text:
Part 0 — Orientation. Why Triton, how to set up, and the first kernel.
Part 1 — Fundamentals. The Triton mental model: programs, blocks, masks, strides, reductions.
Part 2 — Basic NN kernels. Softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, activations. The building blocks.
Part 3 — Matmul. Tiled, batched, and persistent matmul. The workhorse of every transformer.
Part 4 — Attention. The whole attention pipeline, ending in FlashAttention forward, backward, and KV cache.
Part 5 — LLM fusion. Fused residual + norm, fused MLP, cross-entropy, sampling.
Part 6 — Quantization. Low-precision storage and dequant matmul.
Part 7 — Debug, test, profile, optimize. The craft skills you need to ship.
Part 8 — Capstone. Package what you wrote into a mini library, swap it into a real model, and codify your own kernel design playbook.

0.3 A note on the interactive elements
Some chapters include interactive widgets — sliders that show how block sizes tile a tensor, animations that step through the online-softmax accumulator state, plots that compare configurations. These are written as Quarto Observable JS cells and run entirely in your browser. They are there to build intuition; they do not replace running real benchmarks on a real GPU.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
text:
2.1 The landscape: four ways to run math on a GPU
For any operation you want to perform on a GPU, you have roughly four implementation tiers. Each one trades effort for control.
PyTorch eager is what you write by default. y = x @ w + b. Every operator is its own CUDA launch. You pay a fixed launch overhead per op (single-digit microseconds), and every intermediate tensor is materialized in HBM. For training loops dominated by large matmuls this is fine; cuBLAS does the heavy lifting and the launch overhead is amortized. For a long chain of small element-wise ops on a small tensor, the launch tax dominates and you are leaving most of the GPU idle.
torch.compile is the right next step nine times out of ten. It traces your forward (and optionally backward), groups element-wise and reduction ops into fused regions, and lowers them to Triton kernels behind the scenes. You write normal PyTorch; the compiler decides what to fuse. For most workloads where the bottleneck is “too many small ops”, torch.compile solves the problem with zero kernel code. Reach for it first.
Triton is what you use when torch.compile cannot express the fusion you want, when you need an algorithmic rewrite (FlashAttention is the canonical case), or when you want predictable control over tile sizes, accumulator dtypes, and memory layout. You write the kernel in a Python-like DSL. The compiler handles register allocation, instruction scheduling, and the lowering to PTX. You are still working at the tile level, not the thread level.
Raw CUDA is what you use when Triton’s abstractions get in your way: when you need warp-specialization patterns the Triton compiler does not yet expose, when you need WGMMA orchestration that the Hopper backend has not surfaced, or when you are squeezing the last 5% out of a kernel that already runs at 90% of peak. The effort cost jumps by an order of magnitude. For 95% of LLM kernels you will not need it.
The rest of this book lives in the third tier. Before we commit, look at why it exists at all.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
section: 2.2 Why custom kernels matter for LLMs
text:
2.2 Why custom kernels matter for LLMs
A modern decoder-only transformer is mostly two things: matrix multiplications and “everything that connects them”. cuBLAS handles the matmuls — usually well, sometimes excellently. The connective tissue is where Triton earns its keep.
Consider a single transformer block. RMSNorm, then Q/K/V projection, then RoPE, then attention, then output projection, then residual add, then RMSNorm again, then the MLP (up projection, SwiGLU gate, down projection), then another residual add. In eager PyTorch that is roughly 15 distinct kernel launches per block, with several gigabytes of intermediate activations written to HBM and then read back. At inference time, with small batch sizes, the launch overhead alone can exceed the compute time.
Custom kernels let you collapse that chain. Fused residual + RMSNorm becomes one kernel that reads the residual once and the input once, computes the sum and the normalization in registers, and writes the normalized output once. Fused bias + SiLU + multiply (the SwiGLU body) collapses three element-wise passes into one. FlashAttention collapses the entire attention block — Q @ K^T, softmax, P @ V — into a single tiled kernel that never writes the N x N attention matrix to HBM. These are not micro-optimizations. They change the asymptotic memory traffic of the model.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
text:
2.3 What fusion actually does
Fusion is the art of doing more work per byte read from HBM. The mental model is simple: HBM is slow, registers and SRAM are fast, kernel launches have overhead. If you can chain two element-wise ops in registers — read once, compute twice, write once — you halve the memory traffic and remove one launch.
What fuses well: element-wise ops on tensors of the same shape (add, multiply, ReLU, SiLU, sigmoid), broadcasts where one operand is small enough to live in registers, reductions that immediately feed an element-wise op (the softmax pattern: reduce to a max, broadcast back, subtract, exp, reduce to a sum, broadcast back, divide), and matmul-then-element-wise patterns where the element-wise op runs on the matmul tile while it is still in registers (bias add after a GEMM, activation after a GEMM).
What does not fuse easily: ops where the producer’s output shape does not match the consumer’s input layout (e.g., a reduction along axis 0 followed by an operation that needs axis-1 locality), ops separated by a synchronization barrier across the whole tensor (a full softmax cannot fuse with an op that needs the output in row-major order if you computed it in column-major), and anything where the two ops need genuinely different block sizes. torch.compile knows most of these rules and will fuse what it can.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
text:
2.4 Memory bandwidth vs. compute
Every kernel sits on a roofline. The vertical axis is achievable throughput in FLOP/s. The horizontal axis is arithmetic intensity in FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic. The roof has two pieces: a sloped section equal to peak bandwidth times intensity, and a flat section equal to peak FLOPs. The intersection is the ridge point. Kernels to the left of the ridge are memory-bound — their performance is set by how fast you can move bytes. Kernels to the right are compute-bound — their performance is set by the math units.
For an RTX 2070 SUPER, peak HBM bandwidth is roughly 448 GB/s and peak FP16 throughput is roughly 18 TFLOP/s. The ridge point sits near 40 FLOPs per byte. Most LLM kernels that are not matmul live well to the left of that ridge.
The interactive plot below lets you slide an operation’s arithmetic intensity along the roofline. Watch where the dashed line crosses the roof: that is your achievable throughput. Notice how far you have to push intensity before you escape the bandwidth region.

viewof intensity = Inputs.range([0.1, 200], {value: 5, step: 0.1, label: "Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte)"})







peak_bw = 448        // GB/s, RTX 2070 SUPER (approximate)
peak_flops = 18000   // GFLOP/s = 18 TFLOP/s FP16 (approximate)
ridge = peak_flops / peak_bw

roof_xs = d3.range(0.1, 200, 0.5)
roof = roof_xs.map(x => ({
  intensity: x,
  achievable: Math.min(peak_bw * x, peak_flops)
}))

op_point = [{
  intensity: intensity,
  achievable: Math.min(peak_bw * intensity, peak_flops)
}]

bound_label = intensity < ridge ? "memory-bound" : "compute-bound"
achievable_gflops = Math.min(peak_bw * intensity, peak_flops)

Plot.plot({
  width: 720,
  height: 420,
  x: {type: "log", label: "arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte)", domain: [0.1, 200]},
  y: {type: "log", label: "achievable throughput (GFLOP/s) — higher is better", domain: [10, 30000]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(roof, {x: "intensity", y: "achievable", stroke: "steelblue", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([ridge], {stroke: "gray", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.dot(op_point, {x: "intensity", y: "achievable", fill: "crimson", r: 6}),
    Plot.ruleX([intensity], {stroke: "crimson", strokeDasharray: "2,2"}),
    Plot.text([{x: ridge, y: 25000, t: `ridge ≈ ${ridge.toFixed(1)} FLOPs/byte (roof envelope, blue)`}],
              {x: "x", y: "y", text: "t", fill: "gray", textAnchor: "start", dx: 6}),
    Plot.text([{x: intensity, y: achievable_gflops, t: `op point: ${bound_label}, ${(achievable_gflops/1000).toFixed(2)} TFLOP/s`}],

The slider is a toy, but the lesson is real: a kernel with intensity 1 (one FLOP per byte read, like a plain element-wise add) can never run faster than the memory system delivers data, no matter how fast your tensor cores are. If you want that kernel to go faster, you do not optimize the math. You read fewer bytes — by fusing it with its neighbors so the bytes stay in registers.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
text:
2.5 Three motivating examples
Three operations capture the three regimes you will live in for the rest of this book.
RMSNorm — memory-bound. For an input of shape (M, N), RMSNorm reads M * N elements, computes M * N squares, sums them across the row (M reductions of length N), divides by N, takes a reciprocal square root, and writes M * N outputs. The arithmetic per element is a multiply, a squared accumulate, and a multiply-by-scale. Three or four FLOPs per element loaded. Arithmetic intensity is a fraction of one FLOP/byte once you account for the FP16 load width. You will measure RMSNorm performance in fraction of peak HBM bandwidth, never in TFLOP/s. The PyTorch reference for the operation we will rebuild in Chapter 7 is short enough to sit here as an anchor:
def rmsnorm_ref(x: torch.Tensor, weight: torch.Tensor, eps: float = 1e-6) -> torch.Tensor:
    rms = x.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True).add(eps).rsqrt()
    return x * rms * weight
Three lines. The fused Triton version is more lines but performs less memory traffic — one read of x, one read of weight, one write of the output — and that is the whole game.
Matmul — compute-bound. A GEMM with shapes (M, K) times (K, N) reads M*K + K*N elements and performs 2*M*N*K FLOPs. For square shapes around 4096 the arithmetic intensity is in the thousands of FLOPs per byte, well to the right of the ridge. Tensor cores on Ampere and later push FP16 GEMM into the tens of TFLOP/s. Your job in a matmul kernel is not to reduce memory traffic — cuBLAS is already near-optimal on bandwidth. Your job is to keep the tensor cores fed: pick the right tile sizes, accumulate in FP32, use the right num_stages for software pipelining, and avoid bank conflicts. We will spend three chapters on this (Part 3).
Attention — IO-aware algorithmic. Naive attention is the trap that taught the field a lesson. Compute S = Q @ K^T, apply softmax along the last axis, compute O = P @ V. Two matmuls, one softmax. The matmuls are compute-bound; the softmax is memory-bound. But the combination is memory-bound because the N x N matrix S has to be written to HBM after the first matmul and read back for the softmax, and again for the second matmul. For sequence length 8192 that is 64 million entries per head — gigabytes of traffic per layer.
FlashAttention’s insight is not a math change. The math is identical. The change is the schedule: tile the K and V tensors, stream them through the kernel, maintain a running max and a running normalizer per query row, and never write S to HBM at all. The N x N matrix only ever exists in tiles that live in SRAM. Same answer, asymptotically less memory traffic, dramatic speedup on long sequences. We rebuild it in Chapter 14. The point for this chapter is that you cannot get FlashAttention by fusing kernels. You have to rewrite the algorithm with memory hierarchy in mind. That is what Triton lets you do.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
section: 2.6 When not to write a Triton kernel
text:
2.6 When not to write a Triton kernel
Custom kernels are expensive to write, test, and maintain. Do not write one when:

The op is a matmul on standard shapes. cuBLAS is the result of many engineer-years; you will not beat it for general FP16/BF16 GEMM. Use torch.matmul and move on. Write a Triton matmul to learn (Chapter 9), not to ship.
torch.compile already fuses the chain you are worried about. Profile the compiled version first. If the bottleneck moved somewhere else, you are done.
You are still prototyping the model. Iterating on architecture is faster than iterating on kernels. Get the math right in eager mode, then compile, then write a kernel for the one hot spot that remains.
The hot spot is not on the GPU. Tokenization, data loading, host-side bookkeeping — none of these care about Triton.
You do not have a benchmark. Without numbers, “this kernel is faster” is a guess. Always measure against a real PyTorch baseline before claiming a speedup.

The right reflex is: profile, try torch.compile, profile again, and only then reach for Triton — and only for the kernel that actually matters.

title: 2  Chapter 00: Why Triton Exists
section: 2.7 What the rest of the book delivers
text:
2.7 What the rest of the book delivers
This is a tour, not a textbook. Each Part hands you one piece of the picture, ending with a kernel you have written and benchmarked yourself.
Part 1 — Triton Fundamentals. The mental model, pointer arithmetic and strides, reductions. After this Part you can read any simple Triton kernel without staring.
Part 2 — Basic Neural Network Kernels. Fused softmax, LayerNorm, RMSNorm, SwiGLU. Memory-bound kernels where fusion is the whole story.
Part 3 — Matrix Multiplication. Tiled GEMM, batched and linear, persistent matmul. Compute-bound kernels where tile sizing and the accumulator dtype matter.
Part 4 — Attention and Transformer Kernels. Naive attention, FlashAttention forward and backward, RoPE and ALiBi, KV cache. The algorithmic chapters.
Part 5 — Modern LLM Layer Fusion. Fused residual + RMSNorm, fused bias + activation + gate, cross-entropy, sampling. The kernels that make a real serving stack fast.
Part 6 — Quantization-Oriented Kernels. Low-precision storage and dequant-matmul.
Part 7 — Debugging, Testing, Profiling, Optimization. The tooling chapters. Read these out of order whenever you get stuck.
Part 8 — Capstone. Assemble a mini library, replace transformer pieces with your own kernels, and apply the design playbook to a kernel of your choosing.
Next chapter: get your environment running so you can verify each of those kernels on your own GPU. See Chapter 01 for the setup, and the kernel design checklist and LLM kernel map for the running references you will return to.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.1 The dependency graph
Before we start, look at what depends on what. Every step below is one of these arrows.
flowchart LR
    UV[uv] --> PY[Python 3.10+]
    PY --> TORCH[PyTorch CUDA build]
    TORCH --> TRITON[Triton]
    TRITON --> KERNELS[Your kernels]
    CUDA[CUDA driver and runtime] --> TORCH
uv manages Python. PyTorch needs a Python interpreter and the matching CUDA libraries. Triton is either bundled with PyTorch or installed separately; either way, it links against the same CUDA runtime PyTorch uses. Your kernels sit on top.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
section: 3.2 Step 1: install uv and the project environment
text:
3.2 Step 1: install uv and the project environment
This book’s scaffold has already run uv init, so pyproject.toml exists at the repo root. You do not need to run uv init again.
If you do not have uv yet, install it following the upstream instructions at astral.sh/uv. On Linux and macOS the official installer script is the path of least resistance.
Two commands will dominate your workflow:

uv sync — read pyproject.toml and uv.lock, create or update the project’s virtual environment, install everything declared. Run this after cloning the repo and after any pull that touches dependencies.
uv add <package> — add a new dependency, update pyproject.toml and uv.lock, install it. Use this when you want to pull in something new (e.g., uv add matplotlib).

To run a Python file inside the project environment without activating the venv by hand:
uv run python src/ch01_setup/sanity_check.py
uv run resolves the environment and runs the command. You can prepend it to python, pytest, pip, or anything else you would normally run inside an activated venv.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.3 Step 2: install PyTorch with CUDA
PyTorch ships several wheels per release: a CPU-only build, builds for several CUDA versions, and a ROCm build. You want the CUDA build whose major version matches your installed driver. Check what you have:
nvidia-smi
The top-right of the output shows the CUDA version your driver supports. That is the maximum CUDA runtime you can use; you may install a PyTorch wheel built against an equal or lower CUDA version.
Pick the right install command from the official selector at pytorch.org/get-started/locally. The page generates a copy-pasteable command for your OS, package manager, and CUDA version. Do not hardcode a wheel URL from this book — the URLs rotate with each release and the canonical selector always knows the current set.
If you are using uv, install via uv pip install or uv add with the index URL that the PyTorch selector gives you. For example, an Ampere/Turing/Ada machine on Linux with a recent driver typically wants something like (do not copy this literally — check the selector):
uv pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu124
The selector will tell you the exact URL fragment (cu121, cu124, etc.) for your situation.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.4 Step 3: install Triton
Recent PyTorch CUDA builds ship Triton as a transitive dependency. After step 2 you can usually do:
import triton
print(triton.__version__)
If that prints a version, you are done. If you get ModuleNotFoundError, install it explicitly:
uv add triton
Pin a specific version only if you have a reason to — Triton tracks PyTorch fairly closely and the version that came bundled is usually the right one.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
section: 3.5 Step 4: verify the GPU is visible
text:
3.5 Step 4: verify the GPU is visible
The minimum sanity check is below. Save it; we are going to put it in a source file in the next section so you can run it any time.
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

print(torch.__version__)
print(triton.__version__)
print(torch.cuda.get_device_name())
print(torch.cuda.get_device_capability())
Run it with uv run python <path>. You should see:

A non-zero PyTorch version (e.g., 2.5.1+cu124). The +cu124 suffix confirms you got a CUDA build, not the CPU wheel.
A Triton version (e.g., 3.1.0).
Your GPU’s name (e.g., NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 SUPER).
A compute capability tuple (e.g., (7, 5) for the 2070 SUPER’s sm_75).

If torch.cuda.get_device_name() raises an AssertionError saying “Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled”, you installed the CPU wheel. Uninstall it (uv pip uninstall torch) and reinstall with the right index URL.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.6 Step 5: run the first kernel
The rest of the book treats every kernel as a teaching object: shapes, masks, pointer math. Right now we just want to confirm the toolchain end-to-end. The kernel below adds two vectors. It is intentionally minimal — every line will be dissected in Chapter 2.
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offs = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offs < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offs, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offs, x + y, mask=mask)


def vector_add(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, 1024),)
    add_kernel[grid](x, y, out, n, BLOCK_SIZE=1024)
    return out
Smoke test:
x = torch.randn(1_000_003, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
y = torch.randn_like(x)
out = vector_add(x, y)
assert torch.allclose(out, x + y)
print("ok")
The shape 1_000_003 is deliberately not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE. The mask is what keeps the last program from reading or writing past the end of the buffer. We will spend half of Chapter 03 on why that mask matters.
The full file lives at src/ch01_setup/sanity_check.py. Run it:
uv run python src/ch01_setup/sanity_check.py
If the script prints versions, the device name, and ok, your stack is wired up. You can stop reading this chapter and start on Chapter 02.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.7 Platform notes
The book targets Linux + NVIDIA CUDA as the primary path. Other platforms range from fine to painful.

Linux (primary). Works. Any modern NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12.x support and a Turing-generation or newer GPU (sm_75+) will run every kernel in this book. The reference machine is an RTX 2070 SUPER (sm_75); a few chapters in Parts 6 and 7 will flag features that need Ampere/Hopper.
WSL2 (works). Install the NVIDIA WSL driver on the Windows host, then install PyTorch CUDA inside the WSL2 Ubuntu environment exactly as you would on bare Linux. nvidia-smi should work inside WSL once the host driver is set up.
Windows native (don’t). Triton’s Windows support is incomplete and lags upstream. Use WSL2.
macOS (cloud only). There is no CUDA on macOS, so Triton’s CUDA backend cannot run. Use a remote Linux box, a cloud GPU instance, or Google Colab. Edit locally, run remotely.
AMD ROCm (experimental, out of scope). Triton has an upstream ROCm backend under active development. If you have an MI-series GPU and want to experiment, see the Triton GitHub repository for the current status. The kernels in this book assume the CUDA backend; some will work on ROCm with minor changes, others will not.

title: 3  Chapter 01: Environment Setup
text:
3.8 Common installation problems
A short, painful list. If any of these match what you are seeing, the fix is usually quick.

AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled. You installed the CPU wheel. Reinstall PyTorch from the CUDA index URL given by the official selector.
No module named 'triton'. Either you installed a PyTorch build that does not bundle Triton, or your environment got out of sync. Run uv add triton.
CUDA major-version mismatch. Your driver supports CUDA 11.8 but you installed a cu124 wheel. The wheel will load but kernel launches will fail with cryptic errors. Reinstall against the right CUDA major version, or update the driver.
triton and torch versions disagree. Triton’s ABI changes across major releases. If import triton works but triton.jit crashes with an internal error, your torch and triton versions are out of sync. Pin them via uv sync after letting pyproject.toml settle.
Windows native attempts. If you are on Windows and Triton is throwing platform-specific compile errors, stop. Switch to WSL2.
macOS attempts. torch.cuda.is_available() is False on any Mac. Use a remote GPU.
Stale virtual environment. When in doubt, rm -rf .venv && uv sync. uv will rebuild from uv.lock in seconds.

Once sanity_check.py runs end-to-end, you are ready for Chapter 02: the Triton mental model, which dissects the vector_add kernel above line by line.

title: 4  Chapter 2: The Triton Mental Model
text:
4.1 Programs, grids, and launches
A Triton kernel is a Python function decorated with @triton.jit. You launch it from regular PyTorch code by indexing the kernel object with a grid and calling it:
vector_add_kernel[(num_programs,)](x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024)
The grid is a tuple. (N,) is a 1-D grid of N programs. (M, N) is a 2-D grid of M * N programs. Each program is one instance of your kernel and is uniquely identified by a pid (program id) on each axis:
pid   = tl.program_id(axis=0)  # 1-D grid
pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)  # 2-D grid, first axis
pid_n = tl.program_id(axis=1)  # 2-D grid, second axis
If you are used to CUDA, the closest analogy is blockIdx. Unlike CUDA there is no threadIdx — a Triton program is a single SIMD unit, not a collection of cooperating threads. There are no __syncthreads() either. The compiler may emit them under the hood when you do a reduction, but you do not write them.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 2: The Triton Mental Model

title: 4  Chapter 2: The Triton Mental Model
text:
4.2 Tiles, not scalars
Inside the kernel you do not see one element at a time. You see a tile of BLOCK_SIZE elements. Whenever you write tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE), you create a tensor of shape (BLOCK_SIZE,). Whenever you load through that tensor, you get back a tensor. Whenever you add two such tensors, the result is a tensor. The fact that this tensor is implemented as a warp’s worth of registers across some number of warps is the compiler’s problem.
BLOCK_SIZE is a tl.constexpr argument. That is how you tell Triton “this is a compile-time constant; specialize the kernel for this value.” Two different BLOCK_SIZE values produce two different compiled kernels in Triton’s cache. Forgetting to mark a tile dimension constexpr is the first compile error you will hit; the second is forgetting the mask.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 2: The Triton Mental Model

title: 4  Chapter 2: The Triton Mental Model
text:
4.3 A first kernel: vector add
The “hello world” of Triton.

4.3.1 PyTorch reference

def vector_add_ref(x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    return x + y

That is the oracle. Everything below must match it bit-for-bit in fp32 and within rtol=atol=1e-2 in fp16/bf16.


4.3.2 Triton implementation

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def vector_add_kernel(
    x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr,
    n_elements,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements

    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x + y, mask=mask)


def vector_add(x, y, BLOCK_SIZE=1024):
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    grid = (triton.cdiv(x.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE),)
    vector_add_kernel[grid](x, y, out, x.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE)
    return out

The launcher allocates the output, computes the grid as ceil(n / BLOCK_SIZE), and calls the kernel. Note that you pass x (a torch.Tensor) where the kernel expects a *Pointer* — Triton extracts the data pointer automatically. The same is true for y and out.
The kernel body is five lines. pid says which tile this program owns; block_start is the first element index; offsets is the vector [block_start, block_start+1, ..., block_start+BLOCK_SIZE-1]. The mask kills the lanes that fall off the end of the tensor on the tail tile. Load, add, store.


4.3.3 Shape trace
For N = 1_048_576, BLOCK_SIZE = 1024:
Input:                       x, y : (1_048_576,)    fp32
Grid:                        (1024,)
pid = tl.program_id(0)       scalar               int32   # 0 .. 1023
block_start = pid * 1024     scalar offset        int32
offsets = block_start +
          tl.arange(0, 1024) (1024,)              int32   # element indices
mask = offsets < 1_048_576   (1024,)              bool    # all True here
x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets) (1024,)              fp32
y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets) (1024,)              fp32
out = x + y                  (1024,)              fp32
tl.store(out_ptr + offsets,
         out, mask=mask)
For N = 1_000_000, same BLOCK_SIZE: the grid is triton.cdiv(1_000_000, 1024) = 977. Programs 0 through 975 see mask = all True. Program 976 sees mask = offsets < 1_000_000 with exactly 976 * 1024 - 1_000_000 = -23552… wait, the math: 976 * 1024 = 999424 and 977 * 1024 = 1000448, so the last program covers indices [999424, 1000448) and the mask kills the last 1000448 - 1000000 = 448 lanes.
Convince yourself by sliding the widget below to N=17, BLOCK_SIZE=4. You should see exactly 5 programs, and the last one has 3 grey (masked) lanes.

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks
text:
5.1 Storage = buffer + shape + strides
A PyTorch tensor is a triple. There is a 1-D contiguous buffer of bytes in some allocator’s pool, a shape that tells you how many elements there are along each dim, and a stride that tells you how far to move in the buffer when you increment each index by one.
For a 2-D fp32 tensor x of shape (M, N) allocated normally:
The element at x[i, j] lives at byte offset (i * N + j) * 4 in the buffer. x.stride(0) is N and x.stride(1) is 1. Triton inherits this convention: pointer arithmetic is in element units, not bytes, just like PyTorch’s .stride().
This matters when you do x = x.t(). Transpose does not copy the data — it swaps the strides. x.t().shape == (N, M) and x.t().stride() == (1, N). The buffer is still in the original row-major layout; reading x.t() row-by-row therefore reads M non-contiguous addresses per row. If your kernel was written assuming contiguous storage, transposed input will give wrong answers, not just slower answers.

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks

buffer length: M * N * 4 bytes
x.shape == (M, N)
x.stride() == (N, 1) — element units, not bytes

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks
text:
5.2 Pointer arithmetic in Triton
A pointer in Triton is typed by the dtype of the tensor it came from. Adding integer offsets advances the pointer in those elements:
x_ptr        : ptr<fp32>
x_ptr + 1    : ptr<fp32>, one float later, i.e. four bytes
x_ptr + tl.arange(0, 16)  : (16,) ptr<fp32>, sixteen consecutive floats
For 2-D access, broadcast two 1-D ranges:
rows = tl.arange(0, BM)              # (BM,)
cols = tl.arange(0, BN)              # (BN,)
ptrs = x_ptr + rows[:, None] * stride_m + cols[None, :] * stride_n
# ptrs : (BM, BN) ptr<fp32>
If stride_m == N and stride_n == 1, the load is fully contiguous and the GPU can coalesce it into the minimum number of memory transactions. If stride_m == 1 and stride_n == M (a transposed view), every adjacent lane on the same row reads from a different cache line. Same number of elements moved, but multiple times the number of transactions. Bandwidth drops accordingly.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks
text:
5.3 Masks and other=
Every tl.load you write should have a mask. The mask is a boolean tile of the same shape as the offset tile. Lanes where the mask is false do not access memory and return the value of other (default 0). The mask is your safety net against the tail tile and against any conditional access pattern.
The choice of other= matters for downstream code:

For sums, other=0 is the additive identity — masked lanes contribute nothing.
For maxes, other=-inf is the right identity — masked lanes never win.
For products, other=1.
For copies / elementwise, the masked lanes are not used downstream, so the default other=0 is fine.

If you use the wrong other, you can get a kernel that passes the contiguous test (no masked lanes) and silently corrupts the tail tile. The regression test in tests/test_ch04_reductions.py includes a specific case for this.

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks
text:
5.4 Three kernels
This chapter walks through three kernels of increasing structural complexity: 1-D copy, 2-D row add, and 2-D transpose. Each is a small change from the one before; each introduces exactly one new idea.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks

title: 5  Chapter 3: Memory, Pointers, Strides, and Masks
text:
5.5 Kernel 1: 1-D copy
The structural template for everything in the chapter. One program, one tile, load, store.

5.5.1 PyTorch reference

def copy_ref(x):
    return x.clone()



5.5.2 Triton implementation

@triton.jit
def copy_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, x, mask=mask)

Identical in structure to vector_add minus the addition. Use it as a peak-bandwidth probe for your GPU.


5.5.3 Shape trace
Input:                       x : (N,)             fp32
Grid:                        (cdiv(N, BS),)
pid = tl.program_id(0)       scalar               int32
offsets                      (BS,)                int32
mask = offsets < N           (BS,)                bool
tile = tl.load(x_ptr+offsets, mask)   (BS,)       fp32
tl.store(out_ptr+offsets, tile, mask)


5.5.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
Pointers advance in element units; x_ptr + offsets is a (BS,) tile of ptr<fp32>. Mask is the tail-tile guard. other= defaults to 0, which is harmless because we never read the masked lanes of the output.


5.5.5 Correctness test

@pytest.mark.parametrize("n", [7, 1024, 1023, 1025, 1_048_576])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("dtype", [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16])
def test_copy_exact(n, dtype):
    x = torch.randn(n, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    out = copy(x)
    assert torch.equal(out, x)  # bit-exact: no arithmetic happens

Pure copies use torch.equal, not assert_close. There is no rounding to allow for.


5.5.6 Benchmark

ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: copy(x))
gbps = 2 * x.numel() * x.element_size() / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e9  # 1 load + 1 store







Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {N: 4096,     triton_ms: 0.010, torch_ms: 0.012},
    {N: 65536,    triton_ms: 0.015, torch_ms: 0.017},
    {N: 1048576,  triton_ms: 0.070, torch_ms: 0.075},
    {N: 16777216, triton_ms: 1.05,  torch_ms: 1.10},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {N: d.N, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {N: d.N, impl: "torch",  ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {type: "log", label: "N (elements)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "N", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "N", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 5.1: 1-D copy median latency vs tensor length N (log x-axis). Lower is better. Triton copy kernel vs eager torch clone.






5.5.7 Optimization discussion
Bandwidth-bound. BLOCK_SIZE=1024 is fine. Larger BLOCK_SIZE does not help much on a pure copy because each lane already streams from HBM at full bandwidth.


5.5.8 Common bugs

No mask. Tail tile reads past the buffer. Fault or garbage.
BLOCK_SIZE not constexpr. Compile error on tl.arange.
Forgot is_contiguous check in the launcher. The kernel assumes a contiguous buffer; passing x.t() is undetected and gives wrong output.



5.5.9 Exercises
(See exercises/ch03_exercises.md for the kernel-2 / kernel-3 exercises grouped together.)

text:
5.8 Interactive: coalesced vs strided access
Toggle between contiguous and transposed (strided) access. Each cell shows the address one program touches in one load; the colored runs visualize cache-line groupings (one color per cache line of 32 fp32 elements).

viewof N_cells = Inputs.range([4, 64], {value: 16, step: 1, label: "tile width (cells)"})
viewof layout = Inputs.radio(["contiguous", "strided (transposed)"], {value: "contiguous", label: "access pattern"})
viewof stride = Inputs.range([1, 64], {value: 32, step: 1, label: "stride (only used when strided)"})

// --- Derived ------------------------------------------------------------
CACHE_LINE = 32  // fp32 elements per cache line (assumed for the viz)

addresses = {
  const out = [];
  for (let lane = 0; lane < N_cells; lane++) {
    const addr = layout === "contiguous" ? lane : lane * stride;
    out.push({lane: lane, addr: addr, line: Math.floor(addr / CACHE_LINE)});
  }
  return out;
}

distinct_lines = new Set(addresses.map(d => d.line)).size

Plot.plot({
  width: 720,
  height: 120,
  x: {label: "lane (within tile)", domain: [0, N_cells], ticks: d3.range(0, N_cells + 1, Math.max(1, Math.floor(N_cells / 16)))},
  y: {axis: null, domain: [0, 1]},
  color: {legend: true, label: "cache line id (32 fp32 elements per line)", type: "categorical"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect(addresses, {
      x1: d => d.lane,
      x2: d => d.lane + 1,
      y1: 0,
      y2: 1,
      fill: d => d.line,
      stroke: "white",
      strokeWidth: 1,
      title: d => `lane=${d.lane}  addr=${d.addr}  line=${d.line}`
    }),
    Plot.text(addresses, {
      x: d => d.lane + 0.5,
      y: 0.5,
      text: d => d.addr,
      fill: "white",
      fontSize: 10
    })
  ]
})
md`**Distinct cache lines touched:** ${distinct_lines} (out of ${N_cells} lanes). Fewer lines = better coalescing. The contiguous case touches ${Math.ceil(N_cells / CACHE_LINE)} line(s); the strided case touches up to ${N_cells} line(s) when stride ≥ cache-line width.`

Figure 5.6: Address map for one program’s load tile. Each cell is one lane within the tile; the cell color identifies which cache line (32 fp32 elements per line) that lane’s address falls into. Fewer distinct colors means better coalescing; the contiguous case shares colors across lanes, the strided case scatters one color per cell.





5.8.1 Optimization discussion
The kernel is bandwidth bound, but a naive implementation hits maybe 30–60 % of peak because the store side is uncoalesced. To recover the rest you would (a) stage the tile in shared memory with a swizzled layout, (b) write with tl.store of a transposed register tile that aligns to the output’s cache lines. Both are out of scope for this chapter — they belong with matmul. The point of this kernel is to make the read/write asymmetry concrete; the optimization is a later story.


5.8.2 Common bugs

Forgot to swap strides on the output. Writing rows[:, None] * stride_om + cols[None, :] * stride_on instead of the swapped version gives you a copy, not a transpose. The test catches it; the failure mode is “looks like nothing was transposed at all.”
2-D mask built with + or | instead of &. | lets either lane index escape its bound. You write out of range and either fault or corrupt.
BLOCK_M / BLOCK_N too large. A 64x64 tile is 4096 fp32 lanes, which spills registers on smaller GPUs. Start at 32x32.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.1 Why reductions are different
Elementwise kernels are stateless: you stream in, compute, stream out. Reductions are stateful: you must accumulate. Inside a single program instance Triton handles the in-tile reduction for you with tl.sum, tl.max, tl.min, tl.reduce. The hard part is when the axis you want to reduce is bigger than BLOCK_SIZE. Then you must loop, carry a running accumulator, and combine.
The mental model for the rest of this chapter is the same in every kernel:
The choice of identity and combinator changes from kernel to kernel. The skeleton does not.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
One program per output row.
A running scalar (or small vector) accumulator initialized to the identity.
An inner loop over column tiles.
Inside the loop: load tile (with the right other=), reduce in tile, combine with accumulator.
After the loop: post-process (divide by N for mean; sqrt for L2; etc.) and store.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.2 Accumulate in fp32
If the input is fp16 or bf16, promote to fp32 before reducing. A 4096-wide row of N(0, 1) fp16 values has values clustered near ±1; summing them naively in fp16 loses about a bit of precision every doubling, so by the end the running sum has lost roughly log2(4096) = 12 bits. There are 11 bits of mantissa in fp16. You have effectively zero precision left.
The fix is one cast:

x = tl.load(...).to(tl.float32)
acc += tl.sum(x, axis=0)

You will see this pattern in every reduction kernel in the book. Train yourself to spot its absence.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.3 Kernel 1: row-wise sum
out[i] = sum(x[i, :]) for x : (M, N). The simplest reduction. Identity is 0; combinator is +.

6.3.1 PyTorch reference

def row_sum_ref(x):
    return x.sum(dim=1)



6.3.2 Triton implementation

@triton.jit
def row_sum_kernel(
    x_ptr, out_ptr,
    M, N,
    stride_xm, stride_xn,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    x_row = x_ptr + pid_m * stride_xm
    acc = tl.zeros((), dtype=tl.float32)
    for col_start in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        cols = col_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
        mask = cols < N
        x = tl.load(x_row + cols * stride_xn, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        acc += tl.sum(x, axis=0)
    tl.store(out_ptr + pid_m, acc)

tl.zeros(()) creates a 0-d (scalar) accumulator. tl.sum(x, axis=0) collapses the (BLOCK_SIZE_N,) tile to a scalar, and acc += ... accumulates across iterations. The output is always fp32 in this implementation — if you want fp16 output you can cast on the store.


6.3.3 Shape trace
For M=4, N=8192, BLOCK_SIZE_N=1024 in fp16:
Input:                       x   : (4, 8192)        fp16
Output:                      out : (4,)             fp32
Grid:                        (4,)
pid_m                        scalar                 int32
x_row                        scalar ptr<fp16>
acc                          scalar                 fp32  init 0
Inner loop iterations:       8
  cols                       (1024,)                int32
  mask                       (1024,)                bool   # all True here
  x = tl.load(...)           (1024,)                fp16
  x.to(tl.float32)           (1024,)                fp32
  tl.sum(x, axis=0)          scalar                 fp32
  acc                       scalar                 fp32
tl.store(out_ptr+pid_m, acc) writes one scalar


6.3.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
other=0.0 is exactly right: masked lanes contribute 0 to the sum. If you accidentally use other=-inf you will get wrong answers on every kernel where N is not a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE_N and silent passes when it is.


6.3.5 Correctness test

@pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", [(1, 7), (4, 1024), (8, 1025), (32, 1023), (16, 4097), (128, 8192)])
def test_row_sum_fp32(shape):
    x = torch.randn(*shape, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    torch.testing.assert_close(row_sum(x), x.sum(dim=1), rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)

Note the slightly looser rtol=1e-4 versus elementwise — summing many values amplifies the rounding error. For long fp16 rows you can need atol=1e-2 even with fp32 accumulation.


6.3.6 Benchmark

ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: row_sum(x))
# Memory traffic: 1 load per input element + M tiny scalar stores (negligible).
gbps = M * N * x.element_size() / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e9







Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {N: 1024, triton_ms: 0.05, torch_ms: 0.06},
    {N: 2048, triton_ms: 0.09, torch_ms: 0.11},
    {N: 4096, triton_ms: 0.17, torch_ms: 0.20},
    {N: 8192, triton_ms: 0.34, torch_ms: 0.38},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {N: d.N, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {N: d.N, impl: "torch",  ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "N (row width, elements)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "N", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "N", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 6.1: Row-wise sum median latency vs row width N. Lower is better. Triton row_sum kernel vs eager torch.sum(dim=1).






6.3.7 Optimization discussion
Memory bound — one load per element, plus a microscopic store. The compute (one add per element) is free. BLOCK_SIZE_N mostly controls how aggressively the inner loop is unrolled; values between 512 and 4096 are usually within noise of each other. PyTorch’s reference is also memory-bound and the kernels typically come out within 10–20 % of each other.
Further optimization for short rows: drop the inner loop entirely when N <= BLOCK_SIZE_N and let the compiler keep everything in registers. The conditional adds branchy control flow at compile time, which Triton handles fine via tl.constexpr-aware code. We will use that trick in the softmax chapter.


6.3.8 Common bugs

No fp32 cast on low-precision inputs. Silent precision loss; tests on long fp16 rows fail with mysteriously large errors.
Wrong other=. Using -inf or some non-zero constant pollutes the sum on the tail tile.
acc initialized as Python 0.0. Triton requires a typed accumulator: tl.zeros((), dtype=tl.float32). A Python literal triggers a type-mismatch error or, depending on version, silently uses fp16.
Forgot to mask the inner-tile load. Reads past the row, which on a 2-D tensor walks into the next row’s data — your sums are now contaminated with neighboring rows.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.4 Kernel 2: row-wise max
Same skeleton, different identity and combinator. Identity is -inf, combinator is max.

6.4.1 PyTorch reference

def row_max_ref(x):
    return x.amax(dim=1)



6.4.2 Triton implementation

@triton.jit
def row_max_kernel(
    x_ptr, out_ptr,
    M, N,
    stride_xm, stride_xn,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    x_row = x_ptr + pid_m * stride_xm
    NEG_INF = float("-inf")
    acc = tl.full((), NEG_INF, dtype=tl.float32)
    for col_start in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        cols = col_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
        mask = cols < N
        x = tl.load(x_row + cols * stride_xn, mask=mask, other=NEG_INF).to(tl.float32)
        acc = tl.maximum(acc, tl.max(x, axis=0))
    tl.store(out_ptr + pid_m, acc)

other=NEG_INF is doing real work here. If you use the default other=0, then any row whose true max is negative gets corrupted by the masked lanes’ zeros. The dedicated test test_row_max_mask_other_value constructs exactly that case (all-negative input, tail tile) to catch the regression.


6.4.3 Shape trace
Identical structure to row_sum, with acc initialized to -inf and combined with tl.maximum. Skipping the detailed walk-through here — see the row_sum trace and substitute.


6.4.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
The only new idea is other=-inf. Pointer math identical.


6.4.5 Correctness test

def test_row_max_mask_other_value():
    """All-negative input + tail tile — catches the wrong-other=0 bug."""
    x = -torch.rand(4, 1025, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) - 1.0
    out = row_max(x)
    torch.testing.assert_close(out, x.amax(dim=1), rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)



6.4.6 Benchmark

ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: row_max(x))







Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {N: 1024, triton_ms: 0.05, torch_ms: 0.06},
    {N: 2048, triton_ms: 0.09, torch_ms: 0.10},
    {N: 4096, triton_ms: 0.17, torch_ms: 0.19},
    {N: 8192, triton_ms: 0.34, torch_ms: 0.37},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {N: d.N, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {N: d.N, impl: "torch",  ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "N (row width, elements)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "N", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "N", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 6.2: Row-wise max median latency vs row width N. Lower is better. Triton row_max kernel vs eager torch.amax(dim=1).






6.4.7 Optimization discussion
Same story as row_sum. Memory bound, BLOCK_SIZE_N mostly noise. The kernel is the precursor to the online softmax pattern (Chapter 5), where you carry a running (max, sum_of_exps) pair through the same column loop and never write the intermediate max to memory at all.


6.4.8 Common bugs

other=0 on a row of negative values. The 0 becomes the spurious max. The test above catches it.
acc = 0.0. Even with other=-inf on the load, the initial acc value of zero will dominate every row of negatives. Use -inf.
Reducing in fp16. Mostly a precision concern on degenerate inputs; for max the issue is less severe than for sum, but still: promote to fp32.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.6 Kernel 4: row-wise variance
Mean is easy. Variance is where you start having to think.
The textbook identity Var(X) = E[X^2] - E[X]^2 is numerically dangerous when the mean is large relative to the standard deviation. Suppose your row has mean 1e6 and std 1e-3. Then E[X^2] and E[X]^2 are both around 1e12 and their difference is around 1e-6, but each operand is computed with at most fp32 precision (~1e-7 relative), so the subtraction has negative significant digits left. You can get a negative variance, after which sqrt returns NaN and your LayerNorm explodes.
The two-pass approach is bulletproof:

Pass 1: compute the mean.
Pass 2: compute sum((x - mean)^2) / N.

Each pass reads the row from HBM, so the kernel does twice the memory traffic of row_mean. For LayerNorm this is the right trade. In Part 2 we will discuss Welford’s online algorithm as a one-pass alternative; the exercises ask you to implement it.

6.6.1 PyTorch reference

def row_variance_ref(x):
    # population variance (no Bessel correction), matches the kernel.
    return x.var(dim=1, unbiased=False)



6.6.2 Triton implementation

@triton.jit
def row_variance_kernel(
    x_ptr, out_ptr,
    M, N,
    stride_xm, stride_xn,
    BLOCK_SIZE_N: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    x_row = x_ptr + pid_m * stride_xm

    # Pass 1: mean.
    sum_acc = tl.zeros((), dtype=tl.float32)
    for col_start in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        cols = col_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
        mask = cols < N
        x = tl.load(x_row + cols * stride_xn, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        sum_acc += tl.sum(x, axis=0)
    mean = sum_acc / N

    # Pass 2: sum of squared deviations.
    sq_acc = tl.zeros((), dtype=tl.float32)
    for col_start in range(0, N, BLOCK_SIZE_N):
        cols = col_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE_N)
        mask = cols < N
        x = tl.load(x_row + cols * stride_xn, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        diff = tl.where(mask, x - mean, 0.0)
        sq_acc += tl.sum(diff * diff, axis=0)

    tl.store(out_ptr + pid_m, sq_acc / N)

The masked diff is the subtle bit. On the tail tile, tl.load(..., other=0.0) returns 0 for the masked lanes. x - mean on those lanes is -mean, which is not zero, so squaring and summing it would corrupt the variance. The tl.where(mask, x - mean, 0.0) zeros those lanes out before the square. You cannot pass other=mean to tl.load because other must be a compile-time constant; the explicit tl.where is the workaround.


6.6.3 Shape trace
For M=4, N=4096, BLOCK_SIZE_N=1024:
Pass 1:
  sum_acc                    scalar fp32  init 0
  iters: 4
    x = tl.load(...)         (1024,) fp32
    sum_acc += tl.sum(x)     scalar fp32
  mean = sum_acc / N         scalar fp32

Pass 2:
  sq_acc                     scalar fp32  init 0
  iters: 4
    x      = tl.load(...)    (1024,) fp32   # re-read from HBM
    diff   = where(mask, x-mean, 0.0)   (1024,) fp32
    sq_acc += sum(diff*diff) scalar fp32
  tl.store(out+pid_m, sq_acc / N)


6.6.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
Two loops, two loads per element across the kernel as a whole. Pointer math identical to row_mean. other=0 on both loads; the variance-specific subtlety is the tl.where on the diff to zero out masked lanes before squaring.


6.6.5 Correctness test

def test_row_variance_zero_mean_shift():
    """Two-pass variance survives a huge mean shift; naive identity would not."""
    x = torch.randn(4, 4096, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 1e6
    out = row_variance(x)
    assert torch.all(out >= 0)
    torch.testing.assert_close(out, x.var(dim=1, unbiased=False), rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-3)

If you re-implement this kernel with the naive identity, this exact test will fail. It is in the test file specifically as a regression for any attempt to “optimize” the two-pass version into a one-pass E[X^2] - E[X]^2.


6.6.6 Benchmark

ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: row_variance(x))
# Two-pass: 2 loads per element.
gbps = 2 * M * N * x.element_size() / (ms * 1e-3) / 1e9

  const data = [
    {N: 1024, triton_ms: 0.10, torch_ms: 0.12},
    {N: 2048, triton_ms: 0.18, torch_ms: 0.22},
    {N: 4096, triton_ms: 0.34, torch_ms: 0.40},
    {N: 8192, triton_ms: 0.68, torch_ms: 0.78},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {N: d.N, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {N: d.N, impl: "torch",  ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "N (row width, elements)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "N", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "N", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 6.4: Row-wise (two-pass) variance median latency vs row width N. Lower is better. Triton row_variance kernel vs eager torch.var(dim=1, unbiased=False).






6.6.7 Optimization discussion
Two-pass costs 2x the bandwidth of row_mean. The Welford one-pass alternative (exercise A1) cuts that to 1x at the cost of a slightly more expensive per-tile combine. For LayerNorm and RMSNorm in Part 2 we will revisit this trade-off: when you fuse the variance with the affine multiply that follows it, the second read is fused with the data you need anyway, and the two-pass cost disappears.
For now the two-pass approach is the right pedagogical choice: it makes the numerical-stability story concrete and the kernel is short enough to read.


6.6.8 Common bugs

Naive E[X^2] - E[X]^2 identity. Numerically unstable; the shifted-mean test fails.
Forgetting tl.where on the diff for masked lanes. Tail tile contributes spurious mean^2 to the variance.
Reusing sum_acc for sq_acc. Easy typo when you copy-paste pass 1 into pass 2; the variance comes out equal to sum^2 / N^2 and looks plausible enough on small inputs to escape a casual eyeball check.
Computing variance in fp16. The cast to fp32 in this kernel is the whole point of the chapter. Do not skip it.

title: 6  Chapter 4: Reductions
text:
6.7 Looking ahead
These four kernels are the entire vocabulary you need for the next four chapters:

Chapter 5 (softmax): row_max + row_sum (of exps), fused with the elementwise division. The famous online-softmax trick reorders these so you do one pass.
Chapter 6 (LayerNorm): row_mean + row_variance + per-element affine. The two-pass variance kernel above becomes the load-bearing part.
Chapter 7 (RMSNorm): a one-pass reduction (sum of squares) with no mean. Closer to row_l2 from the exercises.
Chapter 20 (cross-entropy): row_max + row_sum + a gather of the target logit.

Get the patterns above into your fingers and the rest of the book becomes “wire these together.”
