title: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation
text:
17.1 Why backward is harder than forward
Forward attention has a tidy structure: each row of Q independently scans K and V, accumulating an output and a running normalizer. The K/V loop can be tiled with no cross-row coordination.
Backward breaks that locality.
Naively materializing [B, H, S, S] for P and dP gives the right answer for tiny S and OOMs by S=4096. The whole point of FlashAttention was to avoid that, and the backward has to avoid it too.
crumbs: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation

title: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation
text:
Softmax backward at row i is dS_i = P_i * (dP_i - rowsum(dP_i * P_i)). The row-sum couples every column to every other column in the same row, so you need the full P_i row in scope when you compute dS_i.
dV is P^T @ dO. The transpose flips the loop nest: now each column of P (i.e. each K row) aggregates contributions from every Q row.
The same gradient (dS) feeds two different reductions: one over j to produce dQ, one over i to produce dK.
crumbs: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation

title: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation
text:
17.2 Two strategies in the literature
Recompute attention during backward. This is FlashAttention v1 and v2. Forward stores O and a per-row scalar L = m + log(sum(exp(s - m))) (log-sum-exp). Backward streams over K/V tiles, recomputes the scores S = Q @ K^T * scale, recovers P = exp(S - L), and uses that to compute partial gradients. You pay extra FLOPs but never materialize P.
Store the attention matrix. Only works when S is so small that the [B, H, S, S] matrix fits in memory and the bandwidth cost is acceptable. Useful for prototyping. Useless past a few hundred tokens.
We use the second strategy for our educational kernel because the chapter is about understanding, not throughput.
crumbs: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation

title: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation
text:
17.3 The gradient math
Given Q, K, V of shape [N, D] (drop batch/head for clarity), scale = 1/sqrt(D), and an upstream gradient dO of shape [N, D]:
S  = Q @ K^T * scale            # [N, N] scores
P  = softmax(S, axis=-1)        # [N, N] probs
O  = P @ V                      # [N, D] output
The gradients flowing back are:
dV = P^T @ dO                                       # [N, D]
dP = dO @ V^T                                       # [N, N]
dS = P * (dP - rowsum(dP * P, keepdim=True))        # [N, N]
dQ = dS @ K * scale                                 # [N, D]
dK = dS^T @ Q * scale                               # [N, D]
The softmax-row Jacobian for one row is J_ij = P_i * (delta_ij - P_j), and dS_i = J_i^T @ dP_i collapses to the formula above. Derive it once with pencil and paper and the rest of the chapter clicks.

title: 17  Chapter 15: Attention Backward — Conceptual and Optional Implementation
text:
17.4 Mapping gradients to kernels
Production Flash backward (see Triton’s 06-fused-attention.py tutorial) splits the work into three kernels:

_attn_bwd_preprocess: computes delta = rowsum(O * dO) per row. This is the same rowsum(dP * P) term, since rowsum(dO @ V^T * P) = rowsum(dO * (P @ V)) = rowsum(dO * O). Caching delta lets the main kernels skip a redundant reduction.
_attn_bwd_dkdv: one program per K/V tile. Loops over Q tiles, recomputes scores, accumulates dV and dK for the owned K/V rows.
_attn_bwd_dq: one program per Q tile. Loops over K/V tiles, recomputes scores, accumulates dQ. (Separating dQ from dKdV avoids cross-program reductions.)

Each kernel reads the per-row L (log-sum-exp) stored by forward and uses it to recover P from S without a fresh max-and-sum pass. Storing L in fp32 is non-negotiable — fp16 loses too many digits for the exponent recovery.
Our educational kernel collapses everything into one straightforward function. Use it to internalize the math, then read the tutorial.

17.4.1 PyTorch reference

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def attention_reference(q, k, v):
    """Standard scaled dot-product attention, no mask, no dropout."""
    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)


def attention_grads_reference(q, k, v, do):
    """Returns (dq, dk, dv) via autograd."""
    q = q.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    k = k.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    v = v.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    o = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    dq, dk, dv = torch.autograd.grad(o, [q, k, v], do)
    return dq, dk, dv



17.4.2 Triton implementation
The educational backward stores P as a [B, H, S, S] tensor in fp32 and runs three small kernels: one for dV, one for dQ, one for dK. Each is essentially a matmul. The point is that you can see, line by line, where the math comes from.

"""
Educational implementation. Not production.
For S > 256 use F.scaled_dot_product_attention, which dispatches to a
proper Flash backward.
"""
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _dv_kernel(
    p_ptr, do_ptr, dv_ptr,
    B, H, S, D,
    stride_pb, stride_ph, stride_pm, stride_pn,
    stride_dob, stride_doh, stride_dom, stride_dod,
    stride_dvb, stride_dvh, stride_dvm, stride_dvd,
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_D: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_bh = tl.program_id(0)
    pid_n  = tl.program_id(1)
    b = pid_bh // H
    h = pid_bh %  H

    offs_n = pid_n * BLOCK_N + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
    offs_d = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_D)

    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D), dtype=tl.float32)
    for m_start in range(0, S, BLOCK_M):
        offs_m = m_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
        # P^T tile: load P[m, n] then implicitly transpose by index order.
        p_ptrs = (
            p_ptr + b * stride_pb + h * stride_ph
            + offs_m[:, None] * stride_pm + offs_n[None, :] * stride_pn
        )
        do_ptrs = (
            do_ptr + b * stride_dob + h * stride_doh
            + offs_m[:, None] * stride_dom + offs_d[None, :] * stride_dod
        )
        m_mask = offs_m < S
        n_mask = offs_n < S
        p  = tl.load(p_ptrs,  mask=m_mask[:, None] & n_mask[None, :], other=0.0)
        do = tl.load(do_ptrs, mask=m_mask[:, None],                   other=0.0)
        # dV[n, d] += sum_m P[m, n] * dO[m, d]
        acc += tl.dot(tl.trans(p), do.to(tl.float32))

    dv_ptrs = (
        dv_ptr + b * stride_dvb + h * stride_dvh
        + offs_n[:, None] * stride_dvm + offs_d[None, :] * stride_dvd
    )
    tl.store(dv_ptrs, acc, mask=(offs_n < S)[:, None])

dQ and dK follow the same shape (full source in src/ch15_attention_backward/educational_backward.py). The launcher first computes P once on the device with a vanilla torch.softmax, then computes dP = dO @ V^T, then dS = P * (dP - rowsum(dP * P, keepdim=True)), then dispatches the kernels for the three matmuls. We let PyTorch do the small pieces and Triton do the GEMM shape so the structure shows clearly.


17.4.3 Shape trace
For the _dv_kernel above (one program owns a (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D) tile of dV):
P:              (B, H, S, S)        fp32
dO:             (B, H, S, D)        fp16
dV:             (B, H, S, D)        fp32 accumulator, fp16 store

Program owns:   one (b, h) and one BLOCK_N slice of dV
pid_bh, pid_n   scalars             int32
b, h            scalars             int32
offs_n          (BLOCK_N,)          int32
offs_d          (BLOCK_D,)          int32
acc             (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D)  fp32

# inner loop, per m tile:
offs_m          (BLOCK_M,)          int32
p  = tl.load    (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_N)  fp32   # P[m, n] tile
do = tl.load    (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_D)  fp16   # dO[m, d] tile
tl.trans(p)     (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_M)  fp32
tl.dot(...)     (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D)  fp32   # accumulates into acc

tl.store(dv)    (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D)  fp32   # masked on offs_n < S


17.4.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
P is logically [B, H, S, S]. We pass per-axis strides so the kernel works on either contiguous or already-transposed layouts. For one (b, h) slice:

b * stride_pb + h * stride_ph selects the head.
offs_m[:, None] * stride_pm + offs_n[None, :] * stride_pn walks the (M, N) plane.
tl.trans(p) is the cheap form of transposing the loaded tile; do not try to load with swapped index order — the strides will be wrong.

Masks: m_mask = offs_m < S and n_mask = offs_n < S handle the non-multiple-of-block edge. other=0.0 is safe because zero contributes nothing to either the matmul (0 * anything = 0) or the subsequent accumulator.


17.4.5 Correctness test

import pytest
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from src.ch15_attention_backward.educational_backward import attention_backward_educational


@pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")
def test_small_grads_match_autograd():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    B, H, S, D = 1, 2, 64, 32
    q = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    k = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    v = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    do = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)

    q_ref = q.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    k_ref = k.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    v_ref = v.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    o_ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q_ref, k_ref, v_ref)
    dq_ref, dk_ref, dv_ref = torch.autograd.grad(o_ref, [q_ref, k_ref, v_ref], do)

    dq, dk, dv = attention_backward_educational(q, k, v, do)
    torch.testing.assert_close(dq, dq_ref, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)
    torch.testing.assert_close(dk, dk_ref, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)
    torch.testing.assert_close(dv, dv_ref, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)



17.4.6 Benchmark
A single timing point is enough for this chapter. The educational backward is much slower than the real Flash backward (which is itself ~3x slower than the forward). Do not chase performance here.

        q_ = q.detach().requires_grad_(True)
        k_ = k.detach().requires_grad_(True)

    torch_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(torch_bwd)
    print(f"educational backward: {edu_ms:.3f} ms")
    print(f"torch SDPA backward : {torch_ms:.3f} ms")

    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    x: {label: "implementation"},
    marks: [Plot.barY(data, {x: "kernel", y: "ms", fill: "kernel"})]
  });
}








Figure 17.1: Attention backward median latency at B=1, H=8, S=256, D=64 fp32. Lower is better. Educational three-kernel Triton backward vs torch SDPA autograd.






17.4.7 Optimization discussion
What the educational kernel leaves on the table:

Materializes P and dP as [B, H, S, S] fp32. Production stores only (O, L) from forward and recomputes P tile-by-tile.
Computes dV, dQ, dK in three separate matmul kernels. Production fuses dK and dV into one kernel that holds a K/V tile in registers and sweeps Q.
Uses fp32 throughout for clarity. Production loads in fp16/bf16, accumulates in fp32, stores in the input dtype.
No causal mask, no varlen, no dropout, no GQA, no head-dim padding. Each of those is its own knob in the real backward.

If you want to push this further, the next step is to drop the materialized P and start streaming. Once you do, you have rebuilt the tutorial — and at that point you should just read it.


17.4.8 Optional: guided reading of the Triton tutorial
The official Triton tutorial at python/tutorials/06-fused-attention.py has a production-ish Flash backward. Skim it in this order:

_attn_bwd_preprocess — computes delta = rowsum(O * dO) per row. Cache for later.
_attn_bwd_dkdv — one program per K/V tile, loops over Q tiles, accumulates dK and dV. Watch how it reads L (the saved log-sum-exp) and recovers P with exp(S - L).
_attn_bwd_dq — one program per Q tile, loops over K/V tiles, accumulates dQ. Same recovery trick.
The launcher — how the three kernels are wired with a single Python-level call.



17.4.9 Common bugs

Forgetting rowsum(dP * P) in the softmax-row Jacobian. The naive dS = P * dP is wrong; you need the row-sum subtraction. Symptom: gradients have the right shape and look “close” for random inputs, but fail an assert_close.
Mixing up P and S. S is pre-softmax scores; P is post-softmax. dV uses P^T, not S^T. Easy to typo, especially in a tile-based kernel where you might have both in scope.
Dropping the 1/sqrt(D) scale in dQ and dK. The scale appears in the forward S = Q @ K^T * scale, so it appears in both dQ = dS @ K * scale and dK = dS^T @ Q * scale. Forgetting one but not the other gives gradients that are off by sqrt(D).
Storing L in fp16. Log-sum-exp can be tens or hundreds in magnitude; fp16 has ~3-4 decimal digits of precision. Keep L in fp32, always.



17.4.10 Exercises
The exercises here are lighter than other chapters and lean on derivations rather than throughput.
Beginner 1. Re-derive the softmax-row Jacobian. Start from p_i = exp(s_i) / sum_j exp(s_j). Differentiate p_i with respect to s_j for both i = j and i != j. Show that the result simplifies to dS_i = P_i * (dP_i - rowsum(dP_i * P_i)). Hint: factor P_i out of the diagonal and off-diagonal cases separately.
Beginner 2. Implement just dV = P^T @ dO as a kernel, given P precomputed on the host. Use the kernel template in src/ch15_attention_backward/educational_backward.py as a starting point. Hint: this is the simplest of the three gradients and a good warm-up for the others.
Beginner 3. Count FLOPs and bytes. For B=1, H=16, S=4096, D=64, estimate the memory cost of storing P as fp32 versus the FLOP cost of recomputing it once during backward. Hint: P is B * H * S * S * 4 bytes; recomputation is 2 * B * H * S * S * D FLOPs for Q @ K^T plus the softmax.
Intermediate 1. Implement dQ as a kernel, given dS precomputed. Mirror the _dv_kernel structure: one program per (b, h, BLOCK_M), loop over K-tiles, accumulate dS @ K * scale. Hint: the loop variable plays the role of the “scan” dimension; do not transpose this one.
Intermediate 2. Read the Triton tutorial’s _attn_bwd_preprocess and explain in a paragraph what it precomputes and why. Hint: look for the identity rowsum(dP * P) = rowsum(dO * O) and ask yourself when each side is cheaper to evaluate.
Advanced. Extend the educational backward to causal=True. The forward causal mask zeros the upper triangle of S before softmax; the backward has to skip the masked positions everywhere. Hint: for dV and dK, the contributing Q rows are only those at positions >= n. For dQ, the contributing K/V rows are only those at positions <= m.

title: 18  Chapter 16: Rotary Positional Embeddings, ALiBi, and Position Kernels
text:
18.1 RoPE in one paragraph
Pair up adjacent dimensions of each head and rotate the pair by an angle that depends on the token position. For dimension pair (2i, 2i+1), the rotation angle at position p is theta_{p, i} = p * base^(-2i/D) (LLaMA uses base = 10000). The rotation is (x, y) -> (x cos - y sin, x sin + y cos). Apply the same rotation to Q and K before the dot product, and the score q · k becomes a function of the relative position (p_q - p_k).
Two layouts circulate. Pick one and document it.
These produce different numbers from the same weights. Mixing them up is the canonical RoPE bug.
crumbs: 18  Chapter 16: Rotary Positional Embeddings, ALiBi, and Position Kernels

title: 18  Chapter 16: Rotary Positional Embeddings, ALiBi, and Position Kernels
text:
Non-interleaved (LLaMA, the most common today): the first half of the head dimension pairs with the second half. Pair i is (x[i], x[D/2 + i]) for i in [0, D/2).
Interleaved (early GPT-J): adjacent dims pair up. Pair i is (x[2i], x[2i+1]).
crumbs: 18  Chapter 16: Rotary Positional Embeddings, ALiBi, and Position Kernels

title: 18  Chapter 16: Rotary Positional Embeddings, ALiBi, and Position Kernels
text:
18.2 ALiBi in one paragraph
Add -m_h * |i - j| to each score in the attention matrix, where m_h is a per-head slope (typically a geometric sequence 2^(-8/H), 2^(-16/H), ...). No sin/cos, no rotation, no extra storage at inference time beyond the slope vector. Trained-with-ALiBi models like BLOOM use it; you cannot retrofit it onto a RoPE-trained model.

18.2.1 PyTorch reference

import torch


def rope_reference(x: torch.Tensor, cos: torch.Tensor, sin: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Non-interleaved RoPE (LLaMA layout).

    x:   [B, H, S, D]
    cos: [S, D/2]
    sin: [S, D/2]
    """
    D = x.shape[-1]
    x1 = x[..., : D // 2]
    x2 = x[...,   D // 2 :]
    # broadcast cos/sin from [S, D/2] to [1, 1, S, D/2]
    cos = cos[None, None, :, :]
    sin = sin[None, None, :, :]
    rot1 = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    rot2 = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return torch.cat([rot1, rot2], dim=-1)


def rope_interleaved_reference(x: torch.Tensor, cos: torch.Tensor, sin: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Interleaved RoPE (GPT-J layout).

    x:   [B, H, S, D]
    cos: [S, D/2]  (same cache as non-interleaved)
    sin: [S, D/2]
    """
    x_even = x[..., 0::2]
    x_odd  = x[..., 1::2]
    cos = cos[None, None, :, :]
    sin = sin[None, None, :, :]
    rot_even = x_even * cos - x_odd * sin
    rot_odd  = x_even * sin + x_odd * cos
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = rot_even
    out[..., 1::2] = rot_odd
    return out


def alibi_bias_reference(num_heads: int, S: int, device, dtype) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Standard ALiBi bias of shape [H, S, S]."""
    # Slopes: geometric sequence, head h has slope 2^(-8h/H) for h in 1..H.
    powers = torch.arange(1, num_heads + 1, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    slopes = torch.pow(2.0, -8.0 * powers / num_heads)
    i = torch.arange(S, device=device)
    rel = (i[:, None] - i[None, :]).abs().to(torch.float32)
    return (-slopes[:, None, None] * rel[None, :, :]).to(dtype)



18.2.2 Triton implementation
One program owns (b, h, m_tile) — a chunk of sequence positions for a single (batch, head). It loads the corresponding rows of cos/sin, applies the rotation, and writes back. The kernel below is the non-interleaved variant with an optional position offset for decoding.

import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _rope_noninterleaved_kernel(
    x_ptr, cos_ptr, sin_ptr, out_ptr,
    B, H, S, D,
    stride_xb, stride_xh, stride_xs, stride_xd,
    stride_ob, stride_oh, stride_os, stride_od,
    stride_cs, stride_cd,
    POS_OFFSET, HALF: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_S: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_bh = tl.program_id(0)
    pid_s  = tl.program_id(1)
    b = pid_bh // H
    h = pid_bh %  H

    offs_s = pid_s * BLOCK_S + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_S)   # token positions inside [0, S)
    offs_h = tl.arange(0, HALF)                        # half-dim indices [0, D/2)
    s_mask = offs_s < S

    # Pointers for x[..., :D/2] and x[..., D/2:]
    base_x = x_ptr + b * stride_xb + h * stride_xh
    x1_ptrs = base_x + offs_s[:, None] * stride_xs + offs_h[None, :] * stride_xd
    x2_ptrs = base_x + offs_s[:, None] * stride_xs + (HALF + offs_h)[None, :] * stride_xd

    # cos/sin indexed by absolute position (offs_s + POS_OFFSET)
    pos = offs_s + POS_OFFSET
    cos_ptrs = cos_ptr + pos[:, None] * stride_cs + offs_h[None, :] * stride_cd
    sin_ptrs = sin_ptr + pos[:, None] * stride_cs + offs_h[None, :] * stride_cd

    x1  = tl.load(x1_ptrs,  mask=s_mask[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    x2  = tl.load(x2_ptrs,  mask=s_mask[:, None], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    cos = tl.load(cos_ptrs, mask=s_mask[:, None], other=0.0)
    sin = tl.load(sin_ptrs, mask=s_mask[:, None], other=0.0)

    rot1 = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    rot2 = x1 * sin + x2 * cos

    base_o = out_ptr + b * stride_ob + h * stride_oh
    o1_ptrs = base_o + offs_s[:, None] * stride_os + offs_h[None, :] * stride_od
    o2_ptrs = base_o + offs_s[:, None] * stride_os + (HALF + offs_h)[None, :] * stride_od
    tl.store(o1_ptrs, rot1.to(x1.dtype), mask=s_mask[:, None])
    tl.store(o2_ptrs, rot2.to(x2.dtype), mask=s_mask[:, None])

The full source — interleaved variant, ALiBi bias kernel, sin/cos cache builder — is in src/ch16_rope/.


18.2.3 Shape trace
For the non-interleaved RoPE kernel above, one program owns one (b, h, BLOCK_S) tile of x:
x:              (B, H, S, D)     fp16   # input
cos, sin:       (S_max, D/2)     fp32   # cache, precomputed at model init
out:            (B, H, S, D)     fp16   # rotated output

Program owns:   one (b, h) and one BLOCK_S slice of x
pid_bh, pid_s   scalars          int32
b, h            scalars          int32
HALF            constexpr        = D / 2
offs_s          (BLOCK_S,)       int32
offs_h          (HALF,)          int32
s_mask          (BLOCK_S,)       bool
pos             (BLOCK_S,)       int32  = offs_s + POS_OFFSET

x1 = tl.load    (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp16 -> fp32
x2 = tl.load    (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp16 -> fp32
cos = tl.load   (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp32
sin = tl.load   (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp32

rot1 = x1*cos - x2*sin           (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp32
rot2 = x1*sin + x2*cos           (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp32

tl.store(o1)    (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp16   # writes x[..., :D/2]
tl.store(o2)    (BLOCK_S, HALF)  fp16   # writes x[..., D/2:]


18.2.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
Two stride games matter.

x and out use the same (stride_b, stride_h, stride_s, stride_d). Letting D be unit-stride means the two halves of the head dim live HALF * stride_d bytes apart. We construct x1_ptrs and x2_ptrs separately rather than loading the full D-wide tile and slicing, because Triton has no clean “slice the last dim in half” primitive.
cos/sin are indexed by absolute position (offs_s + POS_OFFSET). During prefill POS_OFFSET = 0. During decoding, where the program processes one new token at absolute position current_len, you pass POS_OFFSET = current_len and BLOCK_S = 1. This is the one place where the kernel sees “where am I in the cache”.

Masks: s_mask = offs_s < S is the only mask we need. We deliberately make HALF a constexpr and require D to be even, so the half-dim never needs masking.
other=0.0 is safe everywhere: a zeroed x1, x2 rotates to (0, 0), which then gets stored under a False mask anyway.


18.2.5 Correctness test

import pytest
import torch
from src.ch16_rope.rope import rope_noninterleaved, build_cos_sin_cache


@pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")
def test_rope_matches_reference():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    B, H, S, D = 2, 4, 128, 64
    x = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    cos, sin = build_cos_sin_cache(max_seq=S, dim=D, base=10000.0, device="cuda")

    out = rope_noninterleaved(x, cos, sin)

    # Reference
    x1, x2 = x[..., : D // 2].float(), x[..., D // 2 :].float()
    c = cos[None, None, :, :]; s = sin[None, None, :, :]
    ref = torch.cat([x1 * c - x2 * s, x1 * s + x2 * c], dim=-1).to(x.dtype)

    torch.testing.assert_close(out, ref, rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2)



18.2.6 Benchmark

import torch, triton
from src.ch16_rope.rope import rope_noninterleaved, build_cos_sin_cache


def bench(B=2, H=32, S=4096, D=128, dtype=torch.float16):
    x = torch.randn(B, H, S, D, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    cos, sin = build_cos_sin_cache(max_seq=S, dim=D, base=10000.0, device="cuda")

    triton_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: rope_noninterleaved(x, cos, sin))

    def torch_ref():
        x1, x2 = x[..., : D // 2].float(), x[..., D // 2 :].float()
        c = cos[None, None, :, :]; s = sin[None, None, :, :]
        return torch.cat([x1 * c - x2 * s, x1 * s + x2 * c], dim=-1).to(dtype)

    torch_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(torch_ref)
    bytes_moved = 2 * x.numel() * x.element_size()  # read + write
    print(f"triton: {triton_ms:.3f} ms  ({bytes_moved/triton_ms/1e6:.1f} GB/s)")
    print(f"torch : {torch_ms:.3f} ms")







Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {S: 512,  triton_ms: 0.05, torch_ms: 0.18},
    {S: 1024, triton_ms: 0.09, torch_ms: 0.35},
    {S: 2048, triton_ms: 0.18, torch_ms: 0.70},

  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {S: d.S, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},

  ]);

    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "S (sequence length, tokens)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "S", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "S", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 18.1: Non-interleaved RoPE forward median latency vs sequence length S (B=2, H=32, D=128, fp16). Lower is better. Triton kernel vs eager PyTorch reference.






18.2.7 Interactive: RoPE as a coupled rotation
A RoPE pair (x_i, x_{i+D/2}) rotates together like the two coordinates of a single 2D point. Move the position slider to see the rotation angle scale with p * base^(-2i/D). Pairs deeper in the head dim rotate slower.

viewof position = Inputs.range([0, 64], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "position"})
viewof pairIdx  = Inputs.range([0, 31], {value: 0, step: 1, label: "pair index i"})
{
  const base = 10000;
  const D = 64;
  const theta = position * Math.pow(base, -2 * pairIdx / D);
  const x = 1.0, y = 0.0;
  const xr = x * Math.cos(theta) - y * Math.sin(theta);
  const yr = x * Math.sin(theta) + y * Math.cos(theta);
  return Plot.plot({
    aspectRatio: 1,
    x: {domain: [-1.2, 1.2]},
    y: {domain: [-1.2, 1.2]},
    marks: [
      Plot.dot([{x: 0, y: 0}], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: "gray"}),
      Plot.arrow([{x1: 0, y1: 0, x2: xr, y2: yr}], {x1: "x1", y1: "y1", x2: "x2", y2: "y2"}),
      Plot.text([{x: xr, y: yr, label: `theta=${theta.toFixed(2)} rad`}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: "label", dy: -10})
    ]
  });
}












(a)













(b)













(c)






Figure 18.2: RoPE pair rotation viewer. Black arrow shows where the unit vector (1, 0) ends up after rotating by the RoPE angle theta = position * base^(-2i/D) with base=10000, D=64. Pairs deeper in the head dim (higher pair index i) rotate slower at the same position.






18.2.8 Optimization discussion
RoPE is memory-bound: each element is read once, written once, with one multiply-add of arithmetic in between. On an A100 you hit DRAM ceiling at BLOCK_S = 64 to 128 for D = 64 to 128. Beyond that, autotune knobs do nothing.
The real lever is fusion. Chapter 18 and 19 fold RoPE into the Q/K projection: the matmul writes its output tile, rotates it in registers, then stores. You save one full read and one full write of Q and K per token per layer. For a 70B-class model at long context, that is several percent of decode latency.
ALiBi is even cheaper because it has no cache: the slope vector is [H] floats. Inside FlashAttention you compute -slope_h * |i - j| on the fly per tile and add it to the score before the softmax. Materializing [H, S, S] is wasteful — it only makes sense as a debugging step.


18.2.9 Common bugs

Confusing interleaved vs non-interleaved layouts. Both use the same cos/sin cache. Both produce different numbers. If your model’s loss explodes on the first forward pass, this is almost always the cause. Always check the upstream library’s apply_rotary_pos_emb to see which layout it assumes.
Wrong sign on the rotation. The pair is (x cos - y sin, x sin + y cos). Flipping a sign rotates the other direction, which still preserves |q . k| rotational invariance for zero relative position but breaks it elsewhere. Tests on position = 0 will pass; tests on position > 0 will fail.
Wrong position offset for KV-cache decoding. During decode you process one token at absolute position current_len. If you pass POS_OFFSET = 0, the new token gets rotated as if it were the first token. Symptom: the model produces gibberish only at decode, not at prefill. Preview of Chapter 17.
Casting cos/sin to fp16. At S = 8192 and i = 0, theta = 8192 * 1.0 = 8192 rad. sin(8192) is well-defined, but in fp16 the argument loses precision before sin ever runs. Always keep the cache fp32.



18.2.10 Exercises
Beginner 1. Implement non-interleaved RoPE forward as a Triton kernel. Use the kernel and launcher in src/ch16_rope/rope.py as a starting point. Verify against the PyTorch reference on shape [1, 4, 128, 64].
Hint: D must be even. Use a HALF: tl.constexpr = D // 2. Two separate tl.loads for x[..., :HALF] and x[..., HALF:].
Beginner 2. Implement the interleaved variant. The cache is the same; only the indexing changes — adjacent dims pair up. Verify against rope_interleaved_reference.
Hint: use 2 * offs_h and 2 * offs_h + 1 for the even and odd pointers.
Beginner 3. Precompute cos/sin vs compute in-kernel. Write a second kernel variant that computes theta = pos * base^(-2i/D) and the trig inside the kernel. Benchmark against the cached version at S = 1024, 4096. Which wins?
Hint: tl.cos and tl.sin exist. Computing them on the fly trades arithmetic for a DRAM read. For D = 64, the cache is only a few hundred KB.
Intermediate 1. Add a POS_OFFSET argument so a single token at absolute position P during decoding rotates correctly without recomputing the full Q. Test that rope(x[:, :, P:P+1], cos, sin, pos_offset=P) equals rope(x[:, :, :P+1], cos, sin, pos_offset=0)[:, :, P:P+1].
Hint: this is one extra constant added to offs_s before indexing cos/sin. The kernel in src/ch16_rope/rope.py already supports this — re-implement it yourself for understanding.
Intermediate 2. Support partial rotary dims. Some models (e.g. early Phi) rotate only the first rotary_dim of each head dim and pass the rest through. Add a ROTARY_DIM: tl.constexpr parameter; load and rotate [..., :ROTARY_DIM], copy through [..., ROTARY_DIM:].
Hint: the cache becomes [S, ROTARY_DIM / 2]. The pass-through region needs no compute, just a copy — or, if out is x (in-place), no work at all.
Advanced. Fuse RoPE into a Q/K projection kernel. Take a small linear-layer kernel (you can borrow from Chapter 10), have it produce a [B, S, H, D] tile of Q, rotate the tile in-register with RoPE, and store. Compare end-to-end against linear then rope on shape [2, 4096, 32, 128].
Hint: the projection writes its accumulator tile after the K-loop. Insert the rotation just before the store. You will need to load cos/sin once per program at the start.

title: 19  Chapter 17: KV Cache Kernels for Inference
text:
19.1 KV cache layout
A KV cache is a pre-allocated buffer of shape [num_layers, 2, B, H_kv, max_seq, D]. The 2 is K and V. At step t you write the new K and V into position [:, :, :, :, t, :] and then attend against [:, :, :, :, :t+1, :].
Two layouts you will see in the wild:
For this chapter we stick to [B, H, max_seq, D]. The append kernel writes one token’s slice; the decode kernel reads tiles of [B, H, S_chunk, D] against a query of [B, H, 1, D].
crumbs: 19  Chapter 17: KV Cache Kernels for Inference

title: 19  Chapter 17: KV Cache Kernels for Inference
text:
[B, H, S, D] (LLaMA, Mistral). Best when H = H_q = H_kv and the kernel was written for Q of the same shape.
[B, S, H, D] (some inference servers). Better for paged caches because tokens of a request live contiguously across heads.

title: 19  Chapter 17: KV Cache Kernels for Inference
text:
19.2 Append: writing one token

import torch


def append_kv_cache_reference(k_new, v_new, k_cache, v_cache, position):
    """
    k_new, v_new: [B, H, 1, D]
    k_cache, v_cache: [B, H, max_seq, D]  (in/out)
    position: int, the slot to write into
    """
    k_cache[:, :, position : position + 1, :] = k_new
    v_cache[:, :, position : position + 1, :] = v_new

PyTorch handles this with a copy. A Triton kernel reduces launch overhead when you also want to fuse the position write with something else (e.g. RoPE on the cached K, which some inference paths do).

19.2.1 PyTorch reference

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def append_kv_cache_reference(k_new, v_new, k_cache, v_cache, position: int):
    k_cache[:, :, position : position + 1, :] = k_new
    v_cache[:, :, position : position + 1, :] = v_new


def decode_attention_reference(q, k_cache, v_cache, current_len: int):
    """
    q:        [B, H, 1, D]
    k_cache:  [B, H, max_seq, D]
    v_cache:  [B, H, max_seq, D]
    current_len: number of valid tokens in the cache (inclusive of the new one)
    """
    k = k_cache[:, :, :current_len, :]
    v = v_cache[:, :, :current_len, :]
    return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)



19.2.2 Triton implementation
Append kernel. Elementwise, but with stride arithmetic — the K and V cache strides may not equal the strides of the new K and V tensors.

import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _append_kv_kernel(
    k_new_ptr, v_new_ptr,
    k_cache_ptr, v_cache_ptr,
    B, H, D, POSITION,
    stride_knb, stride_knh, stride_kns, stride_knd,
    stride_vnb, stride_vnh, stride_vns, stride_vnd,
    stride_kcb, stride_kch, stride_kcs, stride_kcd,
    stride_vcb, stride_vch, stride_vcs, stride_vcd,
    BLOCK_D: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_bh = tl.program_id(0)
    b = pid_bh // H
    h = pid_bh %  H

    offs_d = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_D)
    d_mask = offs_d < D

    # New K/V live at sequence index 0 (single-token).
    k_new_ptrs = k_new_ptr + b * stride_knb + h * stride_knh + offs_d * stride_knd
    v_new_ptrs = v_new_ptr + b * stride_vnb + h * stride_vnh + offs_d * stride_vnd

    k = tl.load(k_new_ptrs, mask=d_mask, other=0.0)
    v = tl.load(v_new_ptrs, mask=d_mask, other=0.0)

    # Cache slot at sequence index POSITION.
    k_cache_ptrs = (
        k_cache_ptr + b * stride_kcb + h * stride_kch
        + POSITION * stride_kcs + offs_d * stride_kcd
    )
    v_cache_ptrs = (
        v_cache_ptr + b * stride_vcb + h * stride_vch
        + POSITION * stride_vcs + offs_d * stride_vcd
    )
    tl.store(k_cache_ptrs, k, mask=d_mask)
    tl.store(v_cache_ptrs, v, mask=d_mask)

Decode attention kernel. Single-query online softmax across K/V tiles.

@triton.jit
def _decode_attn_kernel(
    q_ptr, k_cache_ptr, v_cache_ptr, out_ptr,
    B, H, CURRENT_LEN, D, scale,
    stride_qb, stride_qh, stride_qs, stride_qd,
    stride_kb, stride_kh, stride_ks, stride_kd,
    stride_vb, stride_vh, stride_vs, stride_vd,
    stride_ob, stride_oh, stride_os, stride_od,
    BLOCK_N: tl.constexpr, BLOCK_D: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_bh = tl.program_id(0)
    b = pid_bh // H
    h = pid_bh %  H

    offs_d = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_D)
    d_mask = offs_d < D

    # Load q (single token).
    q_ptrs = q_ptr + b * stride_qb + h * stride_qh + offs_d * stride_qd
    q = tl.load(q_ptrs, mask=d_mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32) * scale

    m_i = -float("inf")
    l_i = 0.0
    acc = tl.zeros((BLOCK_D,), dtype=tl.float32)

    for n_start in range(0, CURRENT_LEN, BLOCK_N):
        offs_n = n_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N)
        n_mask = offs_n < CURRENT_LEN

        k_ptrs = (
            k_cache_ptr + b * stride_kb + h * stride_kh
            + offs_n[:, None] * stride_ks + offs_d[None, :] * stride_kd
        )
        v_ptrs = (
            v_cache_ptr + b * stride_vb + h * stride_vh
            + offs_n[:, None] * stride_vs + offs_d[None, :] * stride_vd
        )
        k_tile = tl.load(k_ptrs, mask=n_mask[:, None] & d_mask[None, :], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        v_tile = tl.load(v_ptrs, mask=n_mask[:, None] & d_mask[None, :], other=0.0).to(tl.float32)

        # scores: [BLOCK_N]
        s = tl.sum(k_tile * q[None, :], axis=1)
        s = tl.where(n_mask, s, -float("inf"))

        m_new = tl.maximum(m_i, tl.max(s, axis=0))
        alpha = tl.exp(m_i - m_new)
        p = tl.exp(s - m_new)

        acc = acc * alpha + tl.sum(p[:, None] * v_tile, axis=0)
        l_i = l_i * alpha + tl.sum(p, axis=0)
        m_i = m_new

    out = acc / l_i

    out_ptrs = out_ptr + b * stride_ob + h * stride_oh + offs_d * stride_od
    tl.store(out_ptrs, out, mask=d_mask)

We deliberately keep the score reduction as tl.sum(k_tile * q[None, :], axis=1) rather than a tl.dot — for a single-token query, the “matmul” is [BLOCK_N, D] @ [D], which is a plain reduction.


19.2.3 Shape trace
For _decode_attn_kernel (one program per (b, h), scans the cache):
q:              (B, H, 1, D)        fp16   # query for the new token
k_cache:        (B, H, max_seq, D)  fp16   # cache, valid up to CURRENT_LEN
v_cache:        (B, H, max_seq, D)  fp16
out:            (B, H, 1, D)        fp16

Program owns:   one (b, h)
pid_bh          scalar              int32
b, h            scalars             int32
offs_d          (BLOCK_D,)          int32
d_mask          (BLOCK_D,)          bool

q = tl.load     (BLOCK_D,)          fp16 -> fp32, scaled by 1/sqrt(D)

# accumulators
m_i             scalar              fp32   = -inf
l_i             scalar              fp32   = 0
acc             (BLOCK_D,)          fp32   = 0

# K/V loop, per BLOCK_N tile:
offs_n          (BLOCK_N,)          int32
n_mask          (BLOCK_N,)          bool
k_tile, v_tile  (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D)  fp16 -> fp32
s               (BLOCK_N,)          fp32   = k_tile @ q  (one scalar per cache row)
m_new           scalar              fp32
p               (BLOCK_N,)          fp32   = exp(s - m_new)
acc             (BLOCK_N, BLOCK_D) row-wise updated, accumulator
l_i             scalar              fp32   running normalizer
m_i             scalar              fp32   running max

# finalize
out = acc / l_i  (BLOCK_D,)         fp32 -> fp16 store


19.2.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
The append kernel only has a position index in the cache; everything else is a static (b, h, d) walk. The cache stride for the sequence axis (stride_kcs) tells the kernel how far one cache slot is from the next. For a contiguous [B, H, max_seq, D] cache this is D; for a paged cache it would be the block stride times whatever the block table tells you.
The decode kernel adds a sequence-tile loop. n_mask = offs_n < CURRENT_LEN is critical — without it the kernel reads past the end of the valid cache and pollutes the softmax. We mask the scores (not just the loads) with -inf to keep softmax stable; relying on other=0.0 in the load would let those positions contribute exp(0) = 1 to the softmax, which is wrong.
other=0.0 on the V load is fine because masked positions get p = 0 from the score masking, and 0 * anything = 0.


19.2.5 Correctness test

import pytest
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from src.ch17_kv_cache.append_kv_cache  import append_kv_cache
from src.ch17_kv_cache.decode_attention  import decode_attention


@pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")
def test_append_then_attend_matches_reference():
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    B, H, max_seq, D = 1, 4, 32, 32
    k_cache = torch.zeros(B, H, max_seq, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    v_cache = torch.zeros_like(k_cache)

    # Append a sequence of tokens one by one.
    n = 17
    k_history = torch.randn(B, H, n, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    v_history = torch.randn_like(k_history)
    for t in range(n):
        append_kv_cache(k_history[:, :, t : t + 1, :], v_history[:, :, t : t + 1, :], k_cache, v_cache, t)

    # The cache must now match the history.
    torch.testing.assert_close(k_cache[:, :, :n, :], k_history, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)
    torch.testing.assert_close(v_cache[:, :, :n, :], v_history, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)

    # Decode-attention against the cache must match SDPA on the contiguous slice.
    q = torch.randn(B, H, 1, D, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
    out = decode_attention(q, k_cache, v_cache, current_len=n)
    ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k_history, v_history)
    torch.testing.assert_close(out, ref, rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)

section: 19.3 Paged KV cache: the indirection step
text:
19.3 Paged KV cache: the indirection step
vLLM’s PagedAttention slices the cache into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens), allocates blocks from a pool, and gives each request a block table mapping logical positions to physical block indices. This lets:

Two requests share a common prompt prefix by pointing into the same physical blocks (prefix caching).
The serving system avoid memory fragmentation when requests of varying lengths come and go.
Total throughput climb significantly at the cost of slightly more complex kernels.

The mechanical change in the attention kernel is one extra lookup. Instead of:
# contiguous: cache row n is at offset n * stride_s
k_ptrs = k_cache_ptr + ... + offs_n * stride_s + ...
you get:
# paged: for each logical position, look up its physical block,
# then offset within the block.
block_idx = block_table[offs_n // BLOCK_TOKENS]      # which physical block
slot      = offs_n %  BLOCK_TOKENS                   # position inside that block
k_ptrs = k_cache_ptr + block_idx * BLOCK_STRIDE + slot * stride_s + ...
The rest of the kernel — tl.load, masking, softmax — is unchanged. Implementing this end-to-end is exercise 6.

19.3.1 Optimization discussion
Decode-attention is memory-bound. The arithmetic is O(D) flops per cache row; the memory cost is O(D) bytes per cache row. Roofline says you live or die by DRAM bandwidth.
Three knobs that actually move the needle:

BLOCK_N. Bigger tiles reduce launch overhead and amortize the program-side fixed cost (loading Q once, finalizing once). On A100, BLOCK_N = 64 is a reasonable starting point; tune up if the cache is long.
Don’t recast V to fp32 if you can help it. For very long contexts the V loads dominate; keeping them in fp16/bf16 cuts the read in half. Accumulate in fp32, store in fp32, but load in the input dtype.
Multi-program decode. For very long cache and a single (b, h), one program is a bottleneck. Split the K/V dimension across two programs that produce partial (acc, l, m) triples, then a small merge kernel combines them. This is how Flash-Decoding works.

For append_kv_cache, you’re moving 2 * B * H * D elements per call. Launch overhead dominates at small batch — for tiny B*H consider fusing the append into the K-projection kernel instead.


19.3.2 Common bugs

Wrong position argument. Off-by-one or stale current_len writes the new token over a previous one. Symptom: model loops on the same output forever. Always assert position < max_seq in the launcher.
Reading past current_seq_len in decode. Without a n_mask on the scores, garbage in the unused cache slots contributes to the softmax. Symptom: attention outputs change depending on what was in the cache buffer before you started decoding.
Forgetting batch dim in a paged cache lookup. Each request in the batch has its own block table. A batched paged decode passes block_tables[B, max_blocks] and looks up block_tables[b, offs_n // BLOCK_TOKENS]. Easy to drop the b index and end up sharing a cache across requests.
Saving K after RoPE but V before RoPE — or vice versa. RoPE is applied to Q and K only, not to V. The cache stores RoPE’d K and raw V. Mixing these breaks the rotation invariance the model was trained for. Symptom: gibberish that gets worse with longer context.



19.3.3 Exercises
Beginner 1. Write the append kernel. Use the skeleton in src/ch17_kv_cache/append_kv_cache.py. Test it by writing 17 random tokens one at a time and asserting the first 17 slots of the cache equal the input.
Hint: the new K and V are [B, H, 1, D]; the cache slot is at a single sequence index. One program per (b, h) is enough.
Beginner 2. Write a contiguous-gather kernel: given k_cache[B, H, max_seq, D] and current_len, copy k_cache[:, :, :current_len, :] into a fresh contiguous [B, H, current_len, D] buffer. This is not how production does it — production never gathers — but writing the kernel makes the next exercise easier.
Hint: one program per (b, h, BLOCK_S). Mask offs_s < current_len.
Beginner 3. Benchmark append_kv_cache across batch sizes B in (1, 4, 16, 64) for H = 32, D = 128. At which batch size does the kernel become bandwidth-bound vs launch-overhead-bound?
Hint: the bytes moved scale with B; the kernel launch is fixed. The cross-over is roughly where bytes / DRAM_bandwidth > launch_overhead. On an A100 launch overhead is ~5 us.
Intermediate 1. Extend decode_attention to Group-Query Attention (GQA). The Q has H_q heads; the cache has H_kv < H_q heads, with each KV head shared by H_q / H_kv query heads. Modify the launcher to map each query head to the right KV head, or — better — keep one program per (b, h_kv) and have it process all H_q / H_kv query heads that share that KV head, accumulating into separate outputs.
Hint: h_kv = h_q // (H_q / H_kv). The KV pointer arithmetic uses h_kv; the Q pointer arithmetic uses h_q. The second pattern saves cache reads, which are the bandwidth bottleneck.
Intermediate 2. Implement a block-table lookup primitive. Given block_table[B, max_blocks] and a list of logical positions, return the physical-position indices block_table[b, pos // BLOCK_TOKENS] * BLOCK_TOKENS + pos % BLOCK_TOKENS per (b, pos). Just the lookup, no attention.
Hint: this is a gather. One program per (b, BLOCK_POS). Each thread divides and mods by the constexpr BLOCK_TOKENS.
Advanced. Build a tiny paged-decode attention: Q [B, H, 1, D], paged K_cache, V_cache of shape [num_blocks, BLOCK_TOKENS, H, D], block_tables [B, max_blocks], current_lens [B]. The kernel should process one (b, h) per program and stream over blocks using the block table. Verify against a contiguous-cache reference where you build the contiguous cache from the paged one as a host-side gather.
Hint: this combines exercises 2 and 5 — first do the gather to validate your block-table indexing, then push the lookup into the attention kernel itself.

20.1 Why fuse
Run the unfused version and count HBM traffic for a row of width N:
The intermediate tensor t is written and then immediately re-read. On a memory-bound kernel like this one, that round-trip through HBM is most of the runtime. The fused kernel does the add inside the same program that does the variance reduction. Total traffic drops:
You roughly halve the bandwidth bill. The compute is unchanged — these are all elementwise ops plus one reduction.

20.1.1 PyTorch reference

import torch

def residual_rmsnorm_ref(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    residual: torch.Tensor,
    weight: torch.Tensor | None,
    eps: float = 1e-6,
):
    """Reference: rmsnorm(x + residual). Returns (y, x_new).

    x, residual: [..., N], same dtype.
    weight:      [N] or None.
    """
    x_new = x + residual
    # Variance must be computed in fp32 to avoid catastrophic cancellation.
    x32 = x_new.to(torch.float32)
    var = x32.pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    inv_rms = torch.rsqrt(var + eps)
    y = x32 * inv_rms
    if weight is not None:
        y = y * weight.to(torch.float32)
    return y.to(x.dtype), x_new

Two outputs. The downstream attention or MLP block consumes y; the next residual add (a full sub-layer later) consumes x_new. Returning both means the caller does not have to recompute x + residual or stash it before the norm.


20.1.2 Triton implementation
One program per row. The row width N fits in one tile because hidden sizes (4096, 8192) easily fit in a single block on any modern GPU.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _residual_rmsnorm_kernel(
    x_ptr, residual_ptr, weight_ptr, y_ptr, x_new_ptr,
    stride_x_row, stride_r_row, stride_y_row, stride_xn_row,
    N, eps,
    HAS_WEIGHT: tl.constexpr,
    STORE_X_NEW: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = cols < N

    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * stride_x_row + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    r = tl.load(residual_ptr + row * stride_r_row + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    t = x + r

    if STORE_X_NEW:
        tl.store(x_new_ptr + row * stride_xn_row + cols, t, mask=mask)

    var = tl.sum(t * t, axis=0) / N
    inv_rms = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)
    y = t * inv_rms

    if HAS_WEIGHT:
        w = tl.load(weight_ptr + cols, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        y = y * w

    tl.store(y_ptr + row * stride_y_row + cols, y, mask=mask)


def residual_rmsnorm(
    x: torch.Tensor,
    residual: torch.Tensor,
    weight: torch.Tensor | None = None,
    eps: float = 1e-6,
    return_residual: bool = True,
):
    assert x.shape == residual.shape
    assert x.is_cuda and residual.is_cuda
    *batch, N = x.shape
    M = 1
    for d in batch:
        M *= d
    x2 = x.reshape(M, N)
    r2 = residual.reshape(M, N)
    y = torch.empty_like(x2)
    x_new = torch.empty_like(x2) if return_residual else None
    BLOCK_SIZE = triton.next_power_of_2(N)
    grid = (M,)
    _residual_rmsnorm_kernel[grid](
        x2, r2, weight, y, x_new if return_residual else x2,
        x2.stride(0), r2.stride(0), y.stride(0),
        x_new.stride(0) if return_residual else 0,
        N, eps,
        HAS_WEIGHT=weight is not None,
        STORE_X_NEW=return_residual,
        BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE,
    )
    y = y.view_as(x)
    if return_residual:
        return y, x_new.view_as(x)
    return y

Note the STORE_X_NEW constexpr. When the caller does not need the post-add residual, the compiler drops the store entirely. The HAS_WEIGHT constexpr does the same trick for the optional gamma.


20.1.3 Shape trace
Inputs:                    x        : (M, N)     fp16
                           residual : (M, N)     fp16
                           weight   : (N,)       fp16    # or None
Program owns:              one row of x and residual         (axis=0 grid)
pid = tl.program_id(0)     scalar                int32
cols = tl.arange(0, BS)    (BS,)                 int32   # BS = next_pow2(N)
mask = cols < N            (BS,)                 bool
x_ptrs = x_ptr + pid*stride_x_row + cols        (BS,)  ptr<fp16>
x  = tl.load(x_ptrs, mask, other=0.0).to(fp32)  (BS,)  fp32
r  = tl.load(r_ptrs, mask, other=0.0).to(fp32)  (BS,)  fp32
t  = x + r                                       (BS,)  fp32
[opt] tl.store(x_new_ptrs, t, mask)              -      stored fp16 via cast
var     = tl.sum(t*t, axis=0) / N               scalar  fp32
inv_rms = 1.0 / tl.sqrt(var + eps)              scalar  fp32
y = t * inv_rms                                  (BS,)  fp32
[opt] y = y * w   (w cast to fp32)               (BS,)  fp32
tl.store(y_ptrs, y, mask)                        -      stored fp16 via cast
The dtype column is the load-bearing one. Every value that participates in the variance reduction is fp32. Stores cast back to the input dtype because the surface API matches PyTorch.


20.1.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
Strides come from the tensor, not from N. That matters once you start feeding the kernel non-contiguous residuals — the most common case is when the residual was sliced out of a larger activation buffer.
The mask cols < N covers the last partial tile when N is not a power of two. You load with other=0.0 because:

A zero added into x + residual is benign.
A zero squared is zero, which contributes nothing to the variance sum. (Contrast with softmax, where masked-off lanes need -inf so they cannot win the max.)

For the optional x_new store, you must mask the write or you scribble past column N.


20.1.5 Correctness test

import pytest, torch
from ch18_residual_rmsnorm import residual_rmsnorm
from ch18_residual_rmsnorm.residual_rmsnorm import residual_rmsnorm_ref

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", [(2, 7), (4, 1024), (3, 1025), (1, 128), (5, 129)])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("dtype", [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16])
def test_against_ref(shape, dtype):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    M, N = shape
    x = torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    r = torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    w = torch.randn(N, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)

    y_ref, t_ref = residual_rmsnorm_ref(x, r, w)
    y, t = residual_rmsnorm(x, r, w)

    tol = dict(rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2) if dtype != torch.float32 else dict(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)
    torch.testing.assert_close(y, y_ref, **tol)
    torch.testing.assert_close(t, t_ref, **tol)



20.1.6 Benchmark

import torch, triton
from ch18_residual_rmsnorm import residual_rmsnorm

def torch_two_ops(x, r, w, eps=1e-6):
    t = x + r
    var = t.to(torch.float32).pow(2).mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    y = (t.to(torch.float32) * torch.rsqrt(var + eps)).to(x.dtype)
    return y * w, t

torch_compiled = torch.compile(torch_two_ops)

for N in [1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]:
    M = 4096
    x = torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    r = torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    w = torch.randn(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    triton_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: residual_rmsnorm(x, r, w))
    torch_ms  = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: torch_two_ops(x, r, w))
    compiled_ms = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: torch_compiled(x, r, w))
    print(f"N={N}: triton={triton_ms:.3f} torch={torch_ms:.3f} compiled={compiled_ms:.3f}")

    {N: 2048, triton_ms: 0.10, torch_ms: 0.24, compiled_ms: 0.13},
    {N: 4096, triton_ms: 0.20, torch_ms: 0.48, compiled_ms: 0.25},

    marks: [

      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "N", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 20.1: Fused residual + RMSNorm forward median latency vs hidden size N (M=4096). Lower is better. Triton fused kernel vs eager two-op PyTorch vs torch.compile on the same two ops.






20.1.7 Optimization discussion
This kernel is hard memory-bound. Two reads, one or two writes per element, one reduction over N. The roofline says you should hit roughly bandwidth-saturated runtime; if you don’t, look first at warp count, not at the inner math.
Knobs worth a few minutes of autotuning:

num_warps: try 4, 8, 16. Wider hidden sizes prefer more warps.
BLOCK_SIZE: pinned to next_pow2(N) here for simplicity. For very wide rows (N >= 16384) you may need to spill to two passes — see Chapter 7’s discussion.

If you find yourself at 80% of peak HBM bandwidth and want more, the next move is upstream: fuse the kernel with the matmul epilogue that produced x in the first place. That removes another full pass.


20.1.8 Common bugs

Forgetting to return x_new. The caller’s next residual branch needs it. If you return only y, the caller silently recomputes x + residual outside the kernel and you have undone your own fusion.
Casting to fp16 before the variance. t * t in fp16 overflows for activations with magnitude above ~256. Cast t to fp32 before the square, every time. Cast back only at the final store.
Non-contiguous residual. If the caller slices a residual out of a packed buffer, residual.stride(0) is not N. Pass strides in; never hardcode.
Masking the load but not the store. Forgetting the mask on tl.store scribbles past column N and corrupts the next row’s data.



20.1.9 Exercises
Beginner 1 — vanilla return. Modify the launcher so it returns only y (no x_new). Verify with a unit test that the kernel does not store x_new (hint: pass an obviously bad pointer and confirm nothing crashes when STORE_X_NEW=False).
Beginner 2 — both outputs. Use the kernel as-is to return (y, x_new). Assert in a test that x_new matches x + residual exactly when both are fp32.
Beginner 3 — no gamma. Pass weight=None. Confirm the HAS_WEIGHT=False branch produces the same output as RMSNorm with a vector of ones.
Intermediate 1 — drop residual path. Add a drop_residual: bool flag. When True, the kernel ignores residual and behaves like plain RMSNorm (useful for the very first block of the network). Implement with a constexpr so the load is dropped at compile time.
Intermediate 2 — fused dropout. Add dropout between the add and the norm: t = dropout(x + residual, p). Use Triton’s tl.rand for the mask. Test that the expected scaling factor 1 / (1 - p) is applied. Be careful: dropout breaks numerical equality, so use the same RNG seed in the reference.
Advanced — backward kernel. Derive the gradients with respect to x, residual, and weight. The gradient flows through both the add and the norm. Write the backward kernel as a single program-per-row. Compare to torch.autograd on small fp32 inputs.

title: 21  Chapter 19: Fused Bias + Activation + Gate
text:
The LLaMA-family MLP is a three-matmul sandwich:
gate = x @ W_gate.T + b_gate
up   = x @ W_up.T   + b_up
mlp  = (silu(gate) * up) @ W_down.T + b_down
The two outer matmuls are big and compute-bound — leave them to cuBLAS or to the matmul kernel you wrote in Chapter 9. The interesting fusion target is the middle: take gate and up, add biases, apply SiLU, and multiply. Done naively this is three separate elementwise kernels and three HBM round-trips. Fused, it is one read of each, one write, no intermediate materialisation.
This chapter writes that epilogue kernel for both SwiGLU (SiLU gate) and GEGLU (GELU gate).

21.0.1 PyTorch reference

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def swiglu_bias_ref(x_gate, b_gate, x_up, b_up):
    """SiLU(x_gate + b_gate) * (x_up + b_up)."""
    g = x_gate + b_gate
    u = x_up + b_up
    return F.silu(g) * u

def geglu_bias_ref(x_gate, b_gate, x_up, b_up):
    g = x_gate + b_gate
    u = x_up + b_up
    return F.gelu(g, approximate="tanh") * u

Shapes: x_gate, x_up are [M, H] where M = B*T and H is the intermediate dim (typically 11008 or 14336 for 7B-class models). Biases are [H] and broadcast across rows.


21.0.2 Triton implementation
One program per tile of (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_H). The kernel is pure elementwise plus a row-broadcast of the bias.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _swiglu_bias_kernel(
    xg_ptr, bg_ptr, xu_ptr, bu_ptr, y_ptr,
    stride_xg_m, stride_xg_h,
    stride_xu_m, stride_xu_h,
    stride_y_m,  stride_y_h,
    M, H,
    HAS_BG: tl.constexpr,
    HAS_BU: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_M: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK_H: tl.constexpr,
):
    pid_m = tl.program_id(0)
    pid_h = tl.program_id(1)
    offs_m = pid_m * BLOCK_M + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_M)
    offs_h = pid_h * BLOCK_H + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_H)
    mask_m = offs_m < M
    mask_h = offs_h < H
    mask = mask_m[:, None] & mask_h[None, :]

    xg = tl.load(
        xg_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_xg_m + offs_h[None, :] * stride_xg_h,
        mask=mask, other=0.0,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    xu = tl.load(
        xu_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_xu_m + offs_h[None, :] * stride_xu_h,
        mask=mask, other=0.0,
    ).to(tl.float32)

    if HAS_BG:
        bg = tl.load(bg_ptr + offs_h, mask=mask_h, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        xg = xg + bg[None, :]
    if HAS_BU:
        bu = tl.load(bu_ptr + offs_h, mask=mask_h, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
        xu = xu + bu[None, :]

    # SiLU computed in fp32: x * sigmoid(x).
    silu_g = xg * tl.sigmoid(xg)
    y = silu_g * xu

    tl.store(
        y_ptr + offs_m[:, None] * stride_y_m + offs_h[None, :] * stride_y_h,
        y, mask=mask,
    )


def swiglu_bias(x_gate, b_gate, x_up, b_up, BLOCK_M=32, BLOCK_H=128):
    assert x_gate.shape == x_up.shape and x_gate.is_cuda
    M, H = x_gate.shape
    y = torch.empty_like(x_gate)
    grid = (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_M), triton.cdiv(H, BLOCK_H))
    _swiglu_bias_kernel[grid](
        x_gate, b_gate, x_up, b_up, y,
        x_gate.stride(0), x_gate.stride(1),
        x_up.stride(0),   x_up.stride(1),
        y.stride(0),      y.stride(1),
        M, H,
        HAS_BG=b_gate is not None,
        HAS_BU=b_up is not None,
        BLOCK_M=BLOCK_M, BLOCK_H=BLOCK_H,
    )
    return y

The GEGLU variant replaces silu_g with the tanh GELU approximation:

@triton.jit
def _gelu_tanh(x):
    # 0.5 * x * (1 + tanh(sqrt(2/pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x^3)))
    k0 = 0.7978845608028654  # sqrt(2/pi)
    k1 = 0.044715
    inner = k0 * (x + k1 * x * x * x)
    return 0.5 * x * (1.0 + tl.math.tanh(inner))

Same kernel shape, swap the activation. See src/ch19_fused_swiglu/geglu_bias.py.


21.0.3 Shape trace
Inputs:                    x_gate : (M, H)     fp16
                           b_gate : (H,)       fp16   # or None
                           x_up   : (M, H)     fp16
                           b_up   : (H,)       fp16   # or None
Program owns:              one (BLOCK_M, BLOCK_H) tile of the output
pid_m = tl.program_id(0)   scalar              int32
pid_h = tl.program_id(1)   scalar              int32
offs_m = pid_m*BM + arange (BM,)               int32
offs_h = pid_h*BH + arange (BH,)               int32
mask_m, mask_h             (BM,), (BH,)        bool
mask = mask_m & mask_h     (BM, BH)            bool   # via broadcasting
xg = tl.load(xg_ptrs, ...)  (BM, BH)           fp32   # cast on load
xu = tl.load(xu_ptrs, ...)  (BM, BH)           fp32
bg = tl.load(bg, mask_h, ..) (BH,)             fp32
xg = xg + bg[None, :]       (BM, BH)           fp32   # row broadcast
silu_g = xg * sigmoid(xg)   (BM, BH)           fp32
y = silu_g * xu             (BM, BH)           fp32
tl.store(y_ptrs, y, mask)   -                  cast back to fp16
The bias load is (BH,), then broadcast across the M axis via bg[None, :]. This is the natural shape Triton supports — bias broadcasts cost one load per tile column, not one per element.


21.0.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
This is a 2D-tile kernel, so masks are 2D. Build them with mask_m[:, None] & mask_h[None, :]. Without that combination you would either load garbage out of bounds in M or read past the bias buffer in H.
Strides are passed in for both axes of x_gate, x_up, and y. For contiguous row-major tensors stride(0) = H and stride(1) = 1, but never hardcode this — callers may pass slices.
The bias is 1D and uses mask_h alone. other=0.0 is safe here: a zero bias is a no-op when added.


21.0.5 Correctness test

import pytest, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from ch19_fused_swiglu import swiglu_bias, geglu_bias

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("shape", [(7, 13), (64, 11008), (33, 14337)])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("dtype", [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16])
def test_swiglu(shape, dtype):
    M, H = shape
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    xg = torch.randn(M, H, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    bg = torch.randn(H,    device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    xu = torch.randn(M, H, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    bu = torch.randn(H,    device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
    y_ref = F.silu((xg + bg).float()) * (xu + bu).float()
    y_ref = y_ref.to(dtype)
    y = swiglu_bias(xg, bg, xu, bu)
    tol = dict(rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2) if dtype != torch.float32 else dict(rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)
    torch.testing.assert_close(y, y_ref, **tol)



21.0.6 Benchmark

import torch, triton
import torch.nn.functional as F
from ch19_fused_swiglu import swiglu_bias

def torch_unfused(xg, bg, xu, bu):
    return F.silu(xg + bg) * (xu + bu)

for H in [4096, 8192, 11008, 14336]:
    M = 4096
    xg = torch.randn(M, H, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    bg = torch.randn(H,    device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    xu = torch.randn(M, H, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    bu = torch.randn(H,    device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    t = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: swiglu_bias(xg, bg, xu, bu))
    p = triton.testing.do_bench(lambda: torch_unfused(xg, bg, xu, bu))
    print(f"H={H}: triton={t:.3f} torch={p:.3f}")

{
  const data = [
    {H: 4096,  triton_ms: 0.18, torch_ms: 0.55},
    {H: 8192,  triton_ms: 0.34, torch_ms: 1.05},
    {H: 11008, triton_ms: 0.45, torch_ms: 1.40},
    {H: 14336, triton_ms: 0.58, torch_ms: 1.80},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {H: d.H, impl: "triton fused", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {H: d.H, impl: "torch unfused", ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton fused", "torch unfused"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "H (intermediate hidden size, elements)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms, M=4096) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "H", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "H", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 21.1: Fused SiLU(x_gate + b_gate) * (x_up + b_up) median latency vs intermediate hidden size H (M=4096, fp16). Lower is better. Triton fused kernel vs eager unfused PyTorch.






21.0.7 Optimization discussion
Pure memory-bound kernel. The fused traffic is (2 + has_bg + has_bu) * H * sizeof(dtype) read plus M * H * sizeof(dtype) written. The unfused version touches the gate and up tensors three times each.
Knobs:

(BLOCK_M, BLOCK_H): (32, 128) is a reasonable default. For H >= 8192, try (16, 256) to reduce the bias re-load count.
num_warps: 4 to 8 covers most shapes.
Bias caching: the bias is reloaded for each row-tile. If H is small enough that the bias fits in shared memory, you could persist it across tiles via a persistent kernel pattern (see Chapter 11). For LLaMA-scale H = 11008, this is not worth it.

The next-step fusion is to fold this epilogue into the second matmul itself. Triton matmul kernels can apply a post-mma epilogue in-tile, which removes the intermediate gate and up tensors entirely. That is a Chapter 11-level project, not a one-evening exercise.


21.0.8 Common bugs

Bias broadcast direction. bg[None, :] broadcasts across the M axis (correct). Writing bg[:, None] broadcasts the bias across H, which is wrong and produces a kernel that silently runs but gives garbage.
fp16 SiLU at extremes. silu(x) = x * sigmoid(x); in fp16, large positive x saturates the sigmoid to 1 and you lose precision, large negative x produces sigmoid(x) ~ 0 and the multiply underflows. Always cast x to fp32 before the sigmoid, then cast back at the store.
Forgetting the 2D mask. mask_m[:, None] & mask_h[None, :] — both axes, every time. A 1D mask leaves the dead corner of the last tile unmasked.
GELU approximation mismatch. PyTorch’s default F.gelu uses the exact erf-based formula. The tanh approximation differs by up to ~1e-4 even in fp32. If you compare against F.gelu with no approximate argument, the test fails. Use approximate="tanh" on both sides.



21.0.9 Exercises
Beginner 1 — bias + SiLU only. Drop the gate multiplication. Implement silu(x + b) as a one-kernel op. The smallest possible fused kernel in this family.
Beginner 2 — SiLU * gate, no bias. Pass b_gate=None and b_up=None and confirm via the HAS_BG=False / HAS_BU=False constexpr paths.
Beginner 3 — GEGLU. Run the GEGLU variant and compare against F.gelu(g, approximate="tanh") * u. Hint: import tl.math.tanh.
Intermediate 1 — optional biases. Implement a launcher that accepts any combination of b_gate and b_up being None. Verify all four combinations produce correct output.
Intermediate 2 — in-place writeback. Write the result back into x_up to save one allocation. Test that the original x_up is correctly overwritten and that no race conditions exist when the kernel reads x_up after writing it (hint: read first, then store — Triton’s per-program tile lifetime makes this safe).
Advanced — backward kernel. Derive d(x_gate), d(x_up), d(b_gate), d(b_up). The SiLU derivative is silu(x) + sigmoid(x) * (1 - silu(x)). Implement the backward as a single 2D-tile kernel with row-wise atomic adds for the bias gradients.

title: 22  Chapter 20: Cross Entropy and Logits Kernels
text:
The training loop’s outermost loss looks innocent:
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets, ignore_index=-100)
The shape is anything but. logits is [B*T, V] where V is the vocab size — 32k for LLaMA-1, 50k for GPT-2, 128k for LLaMA-3, 256k for the latest Gemma. A [8, 2048, 128000] logits tensor at fp16 is 4.2 GB. Materialising softmax(logits) for the backward pass doubles that. This single op routinely dominates the activation-memory budget of LLM training.
This chapter writes the two kernels that matter:

logsumexp — the row-wise scalar that anchors every softmax-derived loss.
Cross-entropy forward (and optional backward) — fused so you never materialise the softmax tensor.


22.0.1 PyTorch reference

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def cross_entropy_ref(logits, target, ignore_index=-100, reduction="mean"):
    """logits: [N, V]   target: [N]"""
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, target, ignore_index=ignore_index, reduction=reduction)

def logsumexp_ref(logits):
    """Per-row LSE: max + log(sum(exp(x - max)))."""
    return torch.logsumexp(logits, dim=-1)

Manually unrolled for the kernel, per row:
m = max(logits[r])
lse[r] = m + log(sum(exp(logits[r] - m)))
loss[r] = -(logits[r, target[r]] - lse[r])      # if target[r] != ignore_index
        = 0                                      # otherwise
mean_loss = sum(loss) / num_valid_rows


22.0.2 Triton implementation
One program per row. The row’s vocab dimension is tiled by BLOCK_SIZE. For V <= 65536 you can fit the whole row in one tile on most GPUs; for larger vocabs see the chunked-vocab discussion.
logsumexp kernel:

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def _logsumexp_kernel(
    x_ptr, out_ptr,
    stride_x_row,
    N, V,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = cols < V
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * stride_x_row + cols, mask=mask, other=-float("inf")).to(tl.float32)
    m = tl.max(x, axis=0)
    e = tl.exp(x - m)
    # masked-off lanes loaded as -inf -> exp(-inf - m) = 0, safe in the sum.
    s = tl.sum(e, axis=0)
    lse = m + tl.log(s)
    tl.store(out_ptr + row, lse)


def logsumexp(x):
    N, V = x.shape
    out = torch.empty(N, device=x.device, dtype=torch.float32)
    BLOCK_SIZE = triton.next_power_of_2(V)
    _logsumexp_kernel[(N,)](x, out, x.stride(0), N, V, BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE)
    return out

Cross-entropy forward kernel. Same row layout, plus a target gather and an ignore-mask:

@triton.jit
def _ce_forward_kernel(
    logits_ptr, target_ptr, loss_ptr,
    stride_logits_row,
    N, V, ignore_index,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = cols < V

    t = tl.load(target_ptr + row)
    is_valid = t != ignore_index

    x_ptrs = logits_ptr + row * stride_logits_row + cols
    x = tl.load(x_ptrs, mask=mask, other=-float("inf")).to(tl.float32)
    m = tl.max(x, axis=0)
    lse = m + tl.log(tl.sum(tl.exp(x - m), axis=0))

    # Gather logit at the target column. Clamp the index so we never read OOB
    # when the row is ignored.
    safe_t = tl.where(is_valid, t, 0)
    logit_t = tl.load(logits_ptr + row * stride_logits_row + safe_t).to(tl.float32)

    loss = lse - logit_t
    loss = tl.where(is_valid, loss, 0.0)
    tl.store(loss_ptr + row, loss)


def cross_entropy_forward(logits, target, ignore_index=-100, reduction="mean"):
    N, V = logits.shape
    loss = torch.empty(N, device=logits.device, dtype=torch.float32)
    BLOCK_SIZE = triton.next_power_of_2(V)
    _ce_forward_kernel[(N,)](
        logits, target, loss,
        logits.stride(0), N, V, ignore_index,
        BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE,
    )
    if reduction == "none":
        return loss
    num_valid = (target != ignore_index).sum().clamp_min(1)
    if reduction == "sum":
        return loss.sum()
    return loss.sum() / num_valid

Cross-entropy backward. The gradient is softmax(logits) - one_hot(target), divided by num_valid for mean reduction. Compute softmax on the fly — never materialise the full softmax tensor:

@triton.jit
def _ce_backward_kernel(
    dlogits_ptr, logits_ptr, target_ptr, lse_ptr,
    stride_logits_row, stride_dlogits_row,
    N, V, ignore_index, inv_num_valid,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
):
    row = tl.program_id(0)
    cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = cols < V

    t = tl.load(target_ptr + row)
    is_valid = t != ignore_index
    lse = tl.load(lse_ptr + row)

    x = tl.load(logits_ptr + row * stride_logits_row + cols,
                mask=mask, other=-float("inf")).to(tl.float32)
    # softmax = exp(x - lse)
    p = tl.exp(x - lse)
    # subtract the one-hot at the target column
    one_hot = (cols == t).to(tl.float32)
    grad = (p - one_hot) * inv_num_valid
    grad = tl.where(is_valid, grad, 0.0)
    tl.store(dlogits_ptr + row * stride_dlogits_row + cols, grad, mask=mask)

The forward kernel returns LSE alongside the per-row loss (in a fuller implementation), so the backward kernel doesn’t have to recompute it. The chapter’s launcher above computes loss directly; in a full torch.autograd.Function you’d also save LSE for backward.


22.0.3 Shape trace
Inputs:                    logits  : (N, V)     fp16   # N = B*T
                           target  : (N,)       int64
Program owns:              one row of logits and one target id
pid = tl.program_id(0)     scalar               int32
cols = tl.arange(0, BS)    (BS,)                int32   # BS = next_pow2(V)
mask = cols < V            (BS,)                bool

t        = tl.load(target_ptr + pid)            scalar  int64
is_valid = t != ignore_index                    scalar  bool

x_ptrs   = logits_ptr + pid*stride_row + cols   (BS,)   ptr
x        = tl.load(x_ptrs, mask, -inf)          (BS,)   fp32   # cast on load
m        = tl.max(x, axis=0)                    scalar  fp32
e        = tl.exp(x - m)                        (BS,)   fp32   # masked lanes -> 0
s        = tl.sum(e, axis=0)                    scalar  fp32
lse      = m + tl.log(s)                        scalar  fp32

safe_t   = where(is_valid, t, 0)                scalar  int64
logit_t  = tl.load(logits_ptr + pid*sr + safe_t)scalar  fp32
loss_row = lse - logit_t                        scalar  fp32
loss_row = where(is_valid, loss_row, 0.0)       scalar  fp32
tl.store(loss_ptr + pid, loss_row)              -       fp32
The accumulators stay in fp32 throughout. The output is fp32 even when the input is fp16 — fp16 loss values lose too much resolution to be useful for the optimizer.


22.0.4 Pointer arithmetic and masks
Two distinct mask patterns in this kernel:

Vocab mask cols < V. Loaded with other=-inf so masked lanes lose every max and contribute zero to the sum. Confusing the polarity here is the most common bug — other=0.0 would force exp(0 - m) into the sum and inflate the LSE.
Ignore mask t != ignore_index. A per-row scalar, not a per-column vector. Used twice: to guard the target-gather (via safe_t) and to zero the loss output.

The target index is clamped via tl.where(is_valid, t, 0) before the gather. Without the clamp, an ignore_index = -100 would cause the load to walk far outside the logits buffer and either segfault or read garbage that then corrupts the row’s loss.


22.0.5 Correctness test

import pytest, torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from ch20_cross_entropy import cross_entropy_forward, logsumexp

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")

@pytest.mark.parametrize("V", [7, 1024, 1025, 32000, 128000])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("dtype", [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16])

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    logits = torch.randn(N, V, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)

    loss_ref = F.cross_entropy(logits.float(), target, ignore_index=-100)
    tol = dict(rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2) if dtype != torch.float32 else dict(rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4)
    torch.testing.assert_close(loss, loss_ref, **tol)

22.0.7 Optimization discussion
Memory-bound. The kernel reads N * V * 2B (fp16) and writes N * 4B — the read dominates by orders of magnitude. The roofline is HBM bandwidth.
Knobs:

BLOCK_SIZE: pinned to next_pow2(V). For V > 65536 on memory-tight GPUs, this overflows registers — see the chunked-vocab approach below.
num_warps: 8 to 16 for wide vocabs.
Fusing forward + backward: store LSE from forward, reuse in backward. This is the standard torch.autograd.Function pattern. Saves recomputing the row max and sum.

Chunked-vocab pattern. For 256k vocabs, even one row’s worth of fp32 accumulators is 1 MiB. You can do an online softmax (FlashAttention-style) over column chunks: keep a running (max, sum_exp) pair, update with each chunk via the rescaling trick. This trades a small amount of arithmetic for a bounded register budget. See the solutions file for a skeleton.


22.0.8 Common bugs

other=0.0 on the logits load. Masked-off lanes then contribute exp(0 - m) = exp(-m), which is small but nonzero — your LSE drifts. Use -inf.
Forgetting ignore_index. PyTorch defaults to -100. If you don’t handle it, tl.load(logits + row * stride + (-100)) reads upstream into another row or a different buffer entirely.
Wrong reduction. PyTorch’s mean divides by the count of valid rows (target != ignore_index), not by N. Get this wrong and your loss is off by the ignored fraction.
Reading the target logit twice. Some implementations gather the target logit in a separate kernel pass. Do it inside the same row-loop — the logits row is already in registers.



22.0.9 Exercises
Beginner 1 — logsumexp kernel. Implement and test the standalone logsumexp kernel. Compare against torch.logsumexp(x, dim=-1). Use V shapes that exercise the mask.
Beginner 2 — cross-entropy forward without ignore_index. Strip the ignore branch. Simpler kernel, smaller register footprint. Test against F.cross_entropy with default args.
Beginner 3 — add ignore_index back. Take exercise 2’s kernel and add the ignore branch. Verify with a target tensor that mixes valid and -100 entries.
Intermediate 1 — backward kernel. Implement the backward kernel sketched above. Save LSE from forward, pass it to backward. Validate against F.cross_entropy(...).backward().
Intermediate 2 — label smoothing. Implement loss = (1 - eps) * CE + eps * (-mean(log_softmax)). Hint: mean(log_softmax) = -log(V) + (LSE - mean(logits)) — no second softmax pass needed.
Advanced — chunked vocab. Implement online logsumexp using BLOCK_V = 8192 and looping over V in chunks. Maintain a running (running_max, running_sum) pair, update via the rescaling identity s_new = s_old * exp(m_old - m_new) + chunk_sum. Benchmark at V = 256000 against the single-tile kernel.

23.0.1 PyTorch reference
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def sample_ref(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None):
    """logits: [N, V] -> sampled ids [N]."""
    logits = logits / temperature
    if top_k is not None:
        v, _ = torch.topk(logits, top_k, dim=-1)
        threshold = v[:, -1:]
        logits = torch.where(logits < threshold, torch.full_like(logits, -float("inf")), logits)
    if top_p is not None:
        sorted_logits, sorted_idx = torch.sort(logits, descending=True, dim=-1)
        probs = F.softmax(sorted_logits, dim=-1)
        cum = probs.cumsum(dim=-1)
        # mask out entries with cumulative prob > top_p (keeping the first one that crosses)
        mask = cum - probs > top_p
        sorted_logits = sorted_logits.masked_fill(mask, -float("inf"))
        logits = torch.empty_like(logits).scatter_(-1, sorted_idx, sorted_logits)
    probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    return torch.multinomial(probs, 1).squeeze(-1)

def argmax_ref(logits):
    return logits.argmax(dim=-1)
