title: 30  Chapter 28: Build a Mini Triton LLM Kernel Library
text:
You have written something like twenty-five kernels. They live in twenty-five chapter directories. If a colleague asks “can I use your softmax?”, the answer right now is “let me copy a file out of src/ch05_fused_softmax/ and rename it.” That is not a library. This chapter turns the kernels into one.
The goal is a single importable package, mini_triton_llm, that exposes one stable function per kernel. The reader installs it once and writes from mini_triton_llm import rmsnorm from any notebook. We will not invent any new kernels here — we will package the ones you already wrote.

30.0.1 Package layout
src/ch28_mini_lib/
  mini_triton_llm/
    __init__.py            # re-exports the public API
    rmsnorm.py             # Ch 7
    residual_rmsnorm.py    # Ch 18
    softmax.py             # Ch 5
    rope.py                # Ch 16
    swiglu.py              # Ch 19
    attention.py           # Ch 14 (FlashAttention fwd)
    cross_entropy.py       # Ch 20
    benchmarking.py        # Ch 25
    testing.py             # helpers used by the test suite
Three rules guide the layout:

One public function per kernel. No optional kwargs that change the kernel choice. If you need a different kernel, import a different name.
The package is the source of truth. Each module contains the kernel and the launcher in full. Do not import the kernel back from src/chNN_*; those directories are educational scaffolding, not a package.
The public API lives in __init__.py. A user should never need to know which submodule a function lives in.



30.0.2 Public API
__init__.py re-exports everything so the caller types one name:
from mini_triton_llm import (
    rmsnorm,
    residual_rmsnorm,
    softmax,
    rope,
    swiglu,
    flash_attention,
    cross_entropy,
    benchmarking,
    testing,
)
benchmarking and testing are exposed as submodules rather than as flat names because they group several helpers together (bench, compare, assert_close_fp16, random_qkv).


30.0.3 Naming consistency
Across all the modules we follow one set of conventions:

Tensors are PyTorch tensors. No raw torch.cuda.Tensor types in the signature, no .numpy() round trips.
The last dim is the “feature” dim for everything except attention, where the convention is (B, H, S, D).
eps defaults to 1e-6 everywhere it appears.
Kernels validate their inputs and raise ValueError with a message that names the offender. rmsnorm: weight last dim must match x last dim is a useful error; assertion failed is not.



30.0.4 Dtype policy
This is the policy every module enforces:

Input dtype: fp16, bf16, or fp32, depending on the kernel. Documented in the docstring.
Compute dtype: fp32 for reductions, divisions, and softmax exponents. This is the only sane choice and we make it everywhere without asking.
Output dtype: matches the input. The kernel casts on store.

cross_entropy is the one exception: its output is always fp32 because the loss value is a small number and we do not want to round it.


30.0.5 How to use the library
From a notebook:
from mini_triton_llm import rmsnorm

x = torch.randn(4, 1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
w = torch.randn(1024, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
y = rmsnorm(x, w)
For attention:
from mini_triton_llm import flash_attention
from mini_triton_llm.testing import random_qkv

q, k, v = random_qkv(B=2, H=8, S=1024, D=64, dtype=torch.float16)
out = flash_attention(q, k, v, causal=True)
For benchmarking against PyTorch:
from mini_triton_llm import softmax
from mini_triton_llm.benchmarking import compare, print_table

r = compare(
    "softmax",
    lambda: softmax(x),
    lambda: torch.softmax(x.float(), dim=-1).half(),
)
print_table([r])


30.0.6 How to add a new kernel
The mechanical recipe:

Create src/ch28_mini_lib/mini_triton_llm/<new_kernel>.py with the kernel, the launcher, and a one-paragraph docstring.
Add an entry to __init__.py: import the launcher and append its name to __all__.
Add a correctness test to tests/test_ch28_mini_lib.py that imports via the public API (not the submodule) and compares against a PyTorch reference.
Add a benchmark row in benchmarks/bench_ch28_mini_lib.py.

The first chapter exercise walks through this for a geglu kernel.


30.0.7 Correctness test
The package-level test suite is a smoke test, not an exhaustive sweep. The exhaustive sweeps live in the per-chapter test files. The smoke test exists to catch the boring class of bugs: someone renamed a submodule, someone forgot to add a function to __all__, someone changed a kwarg.

import os, sys
import torch, pytest

sys.path.insert(0, "src/ch28_mini_lib")

pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="cuda only")

def test_public_api_imports():
    import mini_triton_llm as mtl
    for name in ["rmsnorm", "residual_rmsnorm", "softmax", "rope",
                 "swiglu", "flash_attention", "cross_entropy",
                 "benchmarking", "testing"]:
        assert hasattr(mtl, name)
    assert mtl.__version__ == "0.1.0"

Each kernel then gets its own short test that re-derives the reference in PyTorch. See tests/test_ch28_mini_lib.py for the full set.


30.0.8 Benchmark
The benchmark file picks one representative shape per kernel and prints a unified table. We do not try to find each kernel’s best shape; we want one number per kernel that is comparable in spirit to the PyTorch reference at the same shape.

from mini_triton_llm import rmsnorm, softmax, swiglu, flash_attention
from mini_triton_llm.benchmarking import compare, print_table
from mini_triton_llm.testing import random_qkv

rows = []
x = torch.randn(4096, 4096, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
w = torch.randn(4096, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda")
rows.append(compare("rmsnorm",
                    lambda: rmsnorm(x, w),
                    lambda: torch.nn.functional.rms_norm(x, (4096,), w)))
rows.append(compare("softmax",
                    lambda: softmax(x),
                    lambda: torch.softmax(x.float(), dim=-1).half()))
print_table(rows)







Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {kernel: "rmsnorm",          triton_ms: 0.18, torch_ms: 0.22},
    {kernel: "residual_rmsnorm", triton_ms: 0.21, torch_ms: 0.30},
    {kernel: "softmax",          triton_ms: 0.30, torch_ms: 0.34},
    {kernel: "rope",             triton_ms: 0.12, torch_ms: 0.18},
    {kernel: "swiglu",           triton_ms: 0.45, torch_ms: 0.55},
    {kernel: "flash_attention",  triton_ms: 1.20, torch_ms: 1.05},
    {kernel: "cross_entropy",    triton_ms: 0.40, torch_ms: 0.60},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {kernel: d.kernel, impl: "triton", ms: d.triton_ms},
    {kernel: d.kernel, impl: "torch",  ms: d.torch_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    marginLeft: 140,
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["triton", "torch"], range: ["steelblue", "orange"]},
    x: {label: "median latency (ms) — lower is better"},
    y: {label: "kernel"},
    fy: {label: "kernel"},
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(long, {fy: "kernel", y: "impl", x: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 30.1: Mini-library kernel median latency at one representative shape per kernel. Lower is better. Triton library implementation vs the matching PyTorch reference.






30.0.9 A note on flash_attention losing
In the placeholder table above, flash_attention runs slightly slower than the PyTorch reference. Read that as a feature of the table, not a defect of your library: PyTorch’s F.scaled_dot_product_attention dispatches to the official flash_attn (or to cuDNN), which is years of tuning past anything you will reproduce in a chapter. The educational kernel exists so you understand what is inside; it does not exist to dethrone the production version.


30.0.10 Exercises
See exercises/ch28_exercises.md. The headline tasks: add a GeGLU kernel (Beginner 1), wire a pyproject.toml and __version__ (Intermediate 5), and wrap rmsnorm in torch.autograd.Function so it supports backward through PyTorch (Advanced 6).

title: 31  Chapter 29: Replace Pieces of a Tiny Transformer
text:
The mini library exists. Now we put it in a transformer. The goal is honest: build a one-layer GPT-style block in plain PyTorch, then build the same block with the Triton kernels from Chapter 28, prove the outputs agree, and report the latency and memory deltas. Some of the deltas will be wins. Some will be wash. One of them will be a loss. We will name each one.

31.0.1 The reference block
A pre-norm transformer block, GPT-style:
x          (B, S, hidden)
|
RMSNorm
|
Q,K,V proj
RoPE on Q, K
Causal multi-head self-attention
O proj
+ x  (residual)
|
RMSNorm
SwiGLU MLP (up_proj -> chunk -> silu * gate -> down_proj)
+ x  (residual)
|
y          (B, S, hidden)
Hidden dim 256, four heads, head dim 64, intermediate dim 1024. Small on purpose: every component is representative of what a real LLM block uses, but the whole thing fits on the author’s 2070 SUPER.
src/ch29_transformer_swap/pytorch_block.py implements this with _rmsnorm_torch (plain PyTorch), _apply_rope_torch, F.scaled_dot_product_attention, and F.silu(a) * b. The linear projections are nn.Linear. Read it; it is intentionally boring.


31.0.2 The Triton block
Same structure, four ops swapped:








Op
Reference
Triton replacement




RMSNorm
_rmsnorm_torch
mini_triton_llm.rmsnorm


RoPE on Q, K
_apply_rope_torch
mini_triton_llm.rope


Causal self-attention
F.scaled_dot_product_attention
mini_triton_llm.flash_attention


SwiGLU activation
F.silu(a) * b
mini_triton_llm.swiglu



Linears stay PyTorch. cuBLAS already wins this race; revisit Chapter 9 if you want a refresher on why we do not reimplement matmul here.
TritonBlock.from_pytorch(ref) clones the reference block’s state_dict so we can swap forwards with identical weights. That is the prerequisite for every correctness test below.


31.0.3 Correctness
Identical weights, identical inputs, outputs close to fp16 tolerances:

from ch29_transformer_swap import BlockConfig, PyTorchBlock, TritonBlock

cfg = BlockConfig(hidden_dim=256, num_heads=4, head_dim=64, intermediate_dim=1024)
ref = PyTorchBlock(cfg, dtype=torch.float16).cuda().eval()
tri = TritonBlock.from_pytorch(ref).cuda().eval()

x = torch.randn(2, 512, 256, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda") * 0.1
with torch.no_grad():
    y_ref = ref(x)
    y_tri = tri(x)

# fp16 end-to-end; loosened from the per-kernel 1e-2 to 3e-2 because of
# the compounding of four kernels' errors.
torch.testing.assert_close(y_tri, y_ref, rtol=3e-2, atol=3e-2)

The looser tolerance is a deliberate choice. Each kernel meets its individual 1e-2 spec; chain four of them through a residual stream and the errors compound. 3e-2 is what a careful reading of “fp16 end-to-end” actually allows.


31.0.4 Latency
Forward time at B=4 and S in {512, 1024, 2048}:

from mini_triton_llm.benchmarking import bench

for S in [512, 1024, 2048]:
    x = torch.randn(4, S, 256, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda") * 0.1
    with torch.no_grad():
        t_torch = bench(lambda: ref(x))
        t_tri = bench(lambda: tri(x))
    print(f"S={S}: torch {t_torch:.3f} ms   triton {t_tri:.3f} ms")

What you will see, roughly:

RMSNorm + SwiGLU win small. Fewer kernel launches, no intermediate silu(a) tensor.
RoPE wins small. PyTorch’s RoPE is several elementwise ops; the Triton version does them in one pass.
Attention is close to a wash, possibly a loss. PyTorch’s SDPA dispatches to the production flash_attn kernel on a recent GPU. Your educational kernel is correct but has had hours of tuning, not years.

The aggregate forward usually comes out a touch faster on Triton, dominated by the fusion wins. Do not expect a 2x. If your benchmark shows a 2x, suspect a bug.


31.0.5 Memory
This is where the Triton path has a real, structural win:

for S in [512, 1024, 2048]:
    x = torch.randn(4, S, 256, dtype=torch.float16, device="cuda") * 0.1
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    with torch.no_grad(): _ = ref(x)
    mb_torch = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / (1024**2)

    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    with torch.no_grad(): _ = tri(x)
    mb_tri = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / (1024**2)
    print(f"S={S}: torch {mb_torch:.1f} MiB   triton {mb_tri:.1f} MiB")

F.scaled_dot_product_attention on a recent PyTorch + GPU will also avoid materializing the [S, S] score matrix (SDPA’s fast path is FlashAttention under the hood). On an older PyTorch, or on a GPU without the fast path, the score matrix is materialized and the torch number grows quadratically with S. Your Triton path stays linear in S because the FlashAttention kernel never writes the score matrix to HBM.
On the same hot path the SwiGLU swap saves one full bandwidth pass over the (B, S, intermediate_dim) silu(a) tensor — at S=2048 and intermediate=1024 that is ~32 MiB per call. Small in this toy block; meaningful in a 32-layer model.






Placeholder data. The numbers below are hardcoded illustrative values, not measurements. Replace with output from your own triton.testing.do_bench run before drawing conclusions.




{
  const data = [
    {S: 512,  torch_ms: 0.55, triton_ms: 0.50, torch_mib: 110, triton_mib: 100},
    {S: 1024, torch_ms: 1.10, triton_ms: 0.95, torch_mib: 220, triton_mib: 200},
    {S: 2048, torch_ms: 2.40, triton_ms: 2.10, torch_mib: 540, triton_mib: 410},
  ];
  const long = data.flatMap(d => [
    {S: d.S, impl: "torch reference", ms: d.torch_ms},
    {S: d.S, impl: "triton swap",     ms: d.triton_ms}
  ]);
  return Plot.plot({
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["torch reference", "triton swap"], range: ["orange", "steelblue"]},
    x: {label: "S (sequence length, tokens)"},
    y: {label: "median latency (ms, B=4) — lower is better"},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(long, {x: "S", y: "ms", stroke: "impl"}),
      Plot.dot(long,  {x: "S", y: "ms", fill: "impl"})
    ]
  });
}








Figure 31.1: One-layer transformer block forward median latency vs sequence length S (B=4 fp16). Lower is better. PyTorch reference block vs the same block with four ops swapped to Triton kernels.






31.0.6 Honesty section
A few things to say plainly:

PyTorch SDPA already dispatches to FlashAttention. The attention-axis “win” you might have expected is not yours to take. Be glad: it means the production version of your kernel exists and works.
Fusion gains are real but small per layer. Multiply by 32 layers in a real model and they add up — but in a one-layer toy they will look unimpressive.
fp16 end-to-end accumulates error. Tolerances of 3e-2 are what the block actually delivers; quote that, not the per-kernel 1e-2.
You did not write a backward kernel. Training this block end-to-end through Triton requires wrapping each launcher in torch.autograd.Function. Exercise 6 walks through it.



31.0.7 Exercises
See exercises/ch29_exercises.md. The headline pieces:

Swap one op at a time (Beginner 1–3) to measure each contribution in isolation.
Stack four layers (Intermediate 4) and see if the wins compound.
Add a KV cache and benchmark decode (Intermediate 5) — this is where the Triton path will pull away.
Wire backward (Advanced 6).

title: 32  Chapter 30: Final Kernel Design Playbook
text:
This is the chapter you will keep coming back to. The previous twenty-nine chapters taught the moves. This one organizes them into a recipe you can follow under deadline, when the layer is unfamiliar and the GPU is unforgiving.
The recipe has fifteen steps. They are in order on purpose. Every shortcut you take here, you pay for in debugging time later — usually at 2 AM, on a Sunday, the day before a deadline.
We walk all fifteen steps using one running example: a fused residual + LayerNorm + dropout kernel. The reference lives at src/ch30_playbook/fused_residual_ln_dropout.py. Read it alongside this chapter.

32.0.1 The fifteen-step playbook

32.0.1.1 1. Write the PyTorch reference
What to do. Write the layer in plain PyTorch. The clearest version you can. No premature optimization. This is your oracle: every test compares against it.
Worked example.

def fused_residual_ln_dropout_ref(x, residual, weight, bias, p, eps):
    h = x + residual                                     # residual stream
    n = F.layer_norm(h, (h.shape[-1],), weight, bias, eps=eps)
    if p > 0:
        m = (torch.rand_like(n) < (1 - p)).to(n.dtype) / (1 - p)
        n = n * m
    return h, n                                          # return both

Common pitfall. “I will skip the reference and tune the Triton kernel directly.” You will spend the next four hours arguing with yourself about whether a 0.003 mismatch is a real bug or a tolerance issue. Write the reference.
Chapter link. Chapter 5 on softmax shows the pattern: PyTorch reference first, Triton second.


32.0.1.2 2. Identify inputs/outputs and their shapes
What to do. Make a table. Tensor name, shape, dtype, role (input / output / scratch). Pin down which dims are batch, which are feature, which are reduced.
Worked example.



name
shape
dtype
role




x
(M, N)
fp16
input


residual
(M, N)
fp16
input


weight
(N,)
fp16
input (param)


bias
(N,)
fp16
input (param)


h
(M, N)
fp16
output (residual)


y
(M, N)
fp16
output (normed)



M = batch * sequence. The kernel does not care; it flattens.
Common pitfall. Forgetting that the kernel produces two outputs. Many fused kernels do.
Chapter link. Chapter 18 (residual + RMSNorm) is the canonical two-output case.


32.0.1.3 3. Identify shape patterns and the reduction axis
What to do. Which dims are mapped over independently? Which dim is reduced (mean, max, sum)? Mapped dims become grid dims; reduced dims become loops or block-wise reductions inside the kernel.
Worked example. The N axis is reduced (mean and variance go over it). The M axis is mapped over: each row’s normalization is independent of every other row.
Common pitfall. Confusing “broadcast” with “reduce”. weight is broadcast across rows (one weight vector for all M); the N axis inside the row is reduced.
Chapter link. Chapter 4 on reductions.


32.0.1.4 4. Decide program/block mapping
What to do. Pick the grid. The default for a row-wise layer is “one program per row”. For 2D tile layers, it is “one program per (row tile, col tile)”. For attention, it is “one program per (batch, head, query tile)”.
Worked example. grid = (M,). One program owns one row. BLOCK_SIZE = next_pow2(N), one block covers the whole row. If N is larger than your hardware’s per-program register/SRAM budget, switch to a multi-block strategy (Chapter 5 covers this for softmax).
Common pitfall. Choosing the grid based on tensor shape alone, then discovering that one program needs more SRAM than the hardware has. Check the register budget early.
Chapter link. Chapter 2 on the mental model; Chapter 7 on RMSNorm for the row-per-program pattern.


32.0.1.5 5. Decide what each program loads
What to do. Enumerate every tl.load. For each, write down what the pointer expression looks like and what mask you will use.
Worked example. One program (row pid) loads:

x[pid, :] — (BLOCK_SIZE,), masked by offs < N, fp16, cast to fp32.
residual[pid, :] — same as above.
weight[:] — (BLOCK_SIZE,), masked, fp16, cast to fp32.
bias[:] — same as weight.

Common pitfall. Loading weight and bias inside an inner loop instead of once at the top of the program. They are tiny; load them once.
Chapter link. Chapter 3 on pointers and strides.


32.0.1.6 6. Decide what each program computes
What to do. Pseudocode the math. Mark every place the dtype changes. Mark every reduction.
Worked example.
h        = x + residual                  (fp32, BLOCK_SIZE)
mean     = sum(h) / N                    (fp32, scalar)
centered = (h - mean) * mask             (fp32, BLOCK_SIZE)
var      = sum(centered ** 2) / N        (fp32, scalar)
inv      = rsqrt(var + eps)              (fp32, scalar)
n        = centered * inv * weight + bias (fp32, BLOCK_SIZE)
if dropout:
    rand = tl.rand(seed, row * BLOCK_SIZE + offs)  (fp32, BLOCK_SIZE)
    n    = n * (rand < p_keep) / p_keep
Common pitfall. Computing centered without masking the out-of-range lanes back to zero before the variance sum. Masked-off lanes will contribute garbage to the reduction.
Chapter link. Chapter 6 on LayerNorm for the mean-then-variance pattern; Chapter 5 for the “shift by max” trick that motivates fp32 in reductions.


32.0.1.7 7. Decide what each program stores
What to do. Two outputs need two tl.stores. Same mask as the input loads.
Worked example.
tl.store(h_ptr + row * stride_hm + offs, h, mask)
tl.store(y_ptr + row * stride_ym + offs, n, mask)
Common pitfall. Forgetting to mask the store and scribbling past the last valid element. Memory checkers will not catch this on power-of-two N; it manifests as a flaky test on N=257.
Chapter link. Chapter 3 on masks.


32.0.1.8 8. Add masks for boundary conditions
What to do. Every load and store touching a partial tile needs mask=. Every reduction whose summand could include masked-off lanes needs other= set to the reduction’s identity (0.0 for sum, -inf for max).
Worked example. mask = offs < N. Load with other=0.0 (because we are summing). The dropout mask uses the same mask; out-of-range lanes are not stored, so their RNG draws are wasted but harmless.
Common pitfall. Using other=0.0 for a max reduction or other=-inf for a sum. The kernel runs, gives wrong answers, and passes any test where N is a multiple of BLOCK_SIZE.
Chapter link. Chapter 3 on masks and other=.


32.0.1.9 9. Decide dtype policy
What to do. Write down: input dtype, accumulator dtype, output dtype. For every reduction, sum in fp32. For softmax exponents, fp32. For matmul accumulator, fp32 unless you have explicit fp64 needs.
Worked example. Input fp16. Compute fp32 (loads cast on read). Output fp16 (stores cast on write). Weight/bias loaded in their stored dtype, cast to fp32 for the multiply-add.
Common pitfall. Accumulating fp16 inputs in fp16. The variance of even moderate-magnitude activations will saturate fp16’s range.
Chapter link. Chapter 7 on RMSNorm spells out the fp32 accumulator policy.


32.0.1.10 10. Test tiny shapes first
What to do. Pick N=7, M=3. Run the kernel. Compare to the reference element-wise. If this fails you cannot debug a larger shape.
Worked example. The Chapter 30 test file’s first case is N=7. It catches mask bugs and stride bugs before anything else.
Common pitfall. Jumping to N=4096 and seeing a 1e-3 deviation, then spending an hour wondering if it is precision or correctness. Start small.
Chapter link. Chapter 24 on debugging.


32.0.1.11 11. Test weird shapes
What to do. Non-power-of-two N (e.g. 511, 1023). N equal to BLOCK_SIZE, BLOCK_SIZE - 1, BLOCK_SIZE + 1. Non-contiguous inputs if you claim to support them (otherwise mark them xfail with a comment).
Worked example. tests/test_ch30_playbook.py parametrizes over N in [7, 64, 511, 1024]. 7 is hand-traceable, 64 is power-of-two, 511 forces the mask, 1024 is the realistic case.
Common pitfall. “It works on N=4096 so it works.” It does not. The mask path is a separate code path and you must exercise it.
Chapter link. Chapter 24 on debugging.


32.0.1.12 12. Benchmark
What to do. triton.testing.do_bench against the PyTorch reference. Same shapes. Median ms. Compute GB/s for memory-bound kernels and TFLOP/s for compute-bound ones. Report both numbers, plus the GPU you ran on.
Worked example. See benchmarks/bench_ch30_playbook.py. Four shapes, fp16, dropout p=0.1. The Triton kernel saves the round-trip of h between the residual op and the LayerNorm, and the round-trip of n between the LayerNorm and the dropout. Both wins are real and measurable.
Common pitfall. Benchmarking the kernel and reporting “10x faster” because PyTorch was running on fp32 and your kernel on fp16. Apples to apples.
Chapter link. Chapter 25 on benchmarking.


32.0.1.13 13. Optimize
What to do. Identify the bound (memory or compute). Try larger BLOCK_SIZE, more num_warps, more num_stages. Look for fusion opportunities with neighboring ops.
Worked example. Our kernel is memory-bound (one read per input byte, one write per output byte). BLOCK_SIZE is already covering the whole row; the knobs left are num_warps (try 2, 4, 8) and potentially fusing the next layer’s residual-add into the same kernel. (At which point you are reinventing Chapter 18.)
Common pitfall. Optimizing before establishing the baseline. Without the baseline you cannot tell whether a change is a 5% win or a 5% loss.
Chapter link. Chapter 27 on perf tuning.


32.0.1.14 14. Autotune
What to do. Wrap the kernel with triton.autotune over a handful of configs that span the realistic shape space. Three to six configs is usually enough. key= should list the shape dims the optimal config depends on.
Worked example. For our kernel:

@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=2),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=4),
        triton.Config({}, num_warps=8),
    ],
    key=["N"],
)

BLOCK_SIZE is computed from N at launch time, so it does not appear in the autotuner.
Common pitfall. Autotuning over fifty configs. Every config adds compile time and warmup overhead. Three to six is usually the sweet spot.
Chapter link. Chapter 26 on autotuning.


32.0.1.15 15. Document limitations
What to do. Docstring on the launcher, in three sections: supported shapes, supported dtypes, known limitations. Add a “future work” note for anything you punted on.
Worked example.
"""
Supported shapes: any (..., N) with N <= 16384.
Supported dtypes: fp16, bf16, fp32.
Limitations:
  - dropout is forward-only; no autograd support.
  - row width N > 16384 will OOM the SRAM; split rows or move to a
    multi-block reduction (Chapter 5 pattern).
"""
Common pitfall. Documenting at launch time and never updating. Update the docstring when you add a feature or hit a regression.
Chapter link. Chapter 25 on benchmark reporting; the checklist in kernel_checklist.qmd.



32.0.2 The checklist, inline
Keep this on your wall. It is the Phase summary of kernel_checklist.qmd.
Phase 1 — Design. Plain-math statement. PyTorch oracle. Shape table. Reduction axis. One-program ownership. Grid shape. Block sizes. Accumulator dtype. SRAM vs registers. Numerical hazards listed.
Phase 2 — Implement. Kernel signature. pid per axis. Offsets from pid * stride. tl.arange per-element. Masks on partial tiles. tl.load with safe other=. Compute. tl.store with mask. Launcher allocates output and validates inputs.
Phase 3 — Test. Tiny shape. Power-of-two. Non-power-of-two. Boundary (BS, BS-1, BS+1). Every dtype. Non-contiguous if supported. Compare to PyTorch with assert_close and dtype-appropriate tolerances.
Phase 4 — Optimize. Baseline. Identify bound. Sweep BLOCK_SIZE. Sweep num_warps. Sweep num_stages. Autotune. Re-measure.
Phase 5 — Document. Signature, shapes, dtypes, hardware. Numerical contract. Benchmark numbers and the GPU.

When you sit down to wire up a new model, this is the lookup table.

The chapter-only kernels are educational scaffolding (the naive attention) or kernels that need more maturation before they belong in a shared library (LayerNorm, persistent matmul, quantized matmul, attention backward).


32.0.4 Where to look next
This book stopped at the kernels you need for a modern transformer forward pass. There is a lot more out there. Pointers:

FlashAttention v3. Asynchronous TMA loads, warp specialization, FP8 compute. Hopper-only.
Persistent kernels with TMA. Chapter 11 introduced persistent; TMA is the H100 instruction that makes the inner loop cheaper.
FP8 training and inference. Chapter 22 introduced the dtype; the production story is transformer_engine and FlashAttention v3.
vLLM internals. The paged KV cache and the continuous-batching scheduler are kernel-level engineering on top of Chapter 17.
AMD ROCm Triton. Triton compiles for AMD. The mental model carries over; the autotune configs do not.

The appendix that follows has a study plan, a list of kernels worth reimplementing from memory, and the capstone challenge. Read it once. Pick one project. Build it.

title: 33  Appendix: Study Plan, Memory Kernels, and the Capstone Challenge
section: 33.2 Kernels You Should Be Able to Write From Memory
text:
33.2 Kernels You Should Be Able to Write From Memory
These are the kernels a Triton-fluent engineer should be able to write into a blank .py file without referring to the book. They cover the patterns; once you have these in your hands, the rest is variations.

vector_add — the hello world.
copy — one read, one write, mask the tail.
row_sum — one program per row, axis-1 reduction.
row_max — same, but with other=-inf.
stable_softmax — row max, shift, exp, row sum, divide.
layernorm_forward — two-pass (mean, var) with affine scale + shift.
rmsnorm_forward — one-pass sum of squares, rsqrt, scale.
gelu — element-wise, tanh-approx form.
silu — element-wise, x * sigmoid(x).
swiglu — element-wise gated: silu(gate) * up.
naive_matmul — square (M = N = K), contiguous, fp16 in / fp32 accumulate / fp16 out, with mask on the K tail.
batched_matmul — same with a leading batch dimension and strides passed in.
rope_forward — paired index addressing with cos/sin tables.
cross_entropy_forward — fused log-softmax + NLL for a single batch row.
flash_attention_forward — simplified, causal, head_dim = 64, one program per (batch, head, query tile), online softmax over K/V tiles.

If you can sit at a blank file and produce all fifteen, you are no longer learning Triton — you are using it.

title: 33  Appendix: Study Plan, Memory Kernels, and the Capstone Challenge
text:
33.3 Self-Assessment Checklist
Tick what you can do without looking it up. Group by stage. Promote yourself only when every box in a tier is checked.

33.3.1 Beginner

Explain the Triton program model: programs, grid, tl.program_id, tl.arange, block sizes.
Explain what a mask is and why you almost always need one on the tail.
Read a 2-D tensor’s strides and translate (i, j) into a pointer offset by hand.
Pick the right other= value for a load that feeds a sum vs a max.
Write a launcher that allocates the output, computes the grid, and calls a kernel.
Pick an appropriate BLOCK_SIZE for a memory-bound elementwise kernel (rule of thumb: 1024–4096).



33.3.2 Intermediate

Explain why the accumulator should be fp32 even when inputs are fp16/bf16, and where exactly to up-cast.
State the shape constraints on tl.dot (multiples of 16, K dim alignment, supported dtype pairs).
Wrap a kernel with triton.autotune and pick a config space that is small, realistic, and pruned.
Derive the online-softmax accumulator state (m, l) and explain the rescaling factor alpha = exp(m - m_new).
Use triton.testing.do_bench correctly: warmup, sync, percentile reporting, GPU named in the writeup.
Distinguish memory-bound from compute-bound for a kernel using rooflines, not vibes.
Walk a stride bug from “tests fail” to “fixed”, using tl.device_print and a tiny-shape test.



33.3.3 Advanced

Reason about FlashAttention’s memory-traffic argument vs naive attention from first principles.
Decide when to fuse two kernels into one and when not to (HBM round-trip math, register pressure).
Pick num_warps and num_stages for a matmul-style kernel with justification, not by random search.
Identify when a kernel is register-bound vs SRAM-bound vs occupancy-bound from the Triton compiler stats.
Build a kernel design plan in the kernel_checklist style without referring to the book.
Explain what changes when you move from sm_75 (Turing) to sm_80 (Ampere) to sm_90 (Hopper) for matmul (bf16, TMA, WGMMA), and why FP8 needs Hopper or newer.

title: 33  Appendix: Study Plan, Memory Kernels, and the Capstone Challenge
text:
33.4 Final Capstone Challenge
The last bar between “I have read a Triton book” and “I write Triton kernels for transformer/LLM work” is a measurable, end-to-end task.

33.4.1 The task
Implement a complete mini transformer block forward pass using your mini_triton_llm library (Chapter 28). Run it as a 4-layer, 256-hidden, 4-head, GPT-style stack with batch=4, seq=1024, fp16. Match a PyTorch reference numerically. Beat or tie PyTorch eager on a 2070 SUPER for end-to-end forward latency.


33.4.2 Success criteria

Correctness. End-to-end output matches a PyTorch reference with rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2 in fp16.
Determinism. Two runs on the same input give bitwise identical output.
Performance. Median wall-clock latency (over 100 runs, after 50 warmup, with torch.cuda.synchronize before/after) is within +/- 10% of PyTorch eager on a 2070 SUPER. Better is better; tied is acceptable; >20% slower means you have work to do.
Reportage. A short writeup (one page) listing: GPU, dtype, batch/seq/hidden, the three kernels you wrote, the three kernels you swapped from torch.nn.functional, where you tied, where you won, where you lost, and a one-sentence theory per loss.



33.4.3 Hints

Start with the mini_triton_llm.attention.flash_attention_forward kernel as the centerpiece. That is where the win is.
Fuse residual + RMSNorm (Chapter 18). That kernel pays for itself once you call it twice per layer.
Leave the two big matmuls (Q/K/V projection, output projection) to torch.matmul / cuBLAS. You will not beat them on a 2070 SUPER. The win is in the things between the matmuls.
For SwiGLU, fuse silu(gate) * up (Chapter 19) but leave the surrounding linears to cuBLAS.
Profile both implementations with do_bench and break latency down per layer. Do not write “Triton is faster” without per-kernel numbers.



33.4.4 What honest losses look like
You will probably lose on:

Standalone Linear / matmul. cuBLAS is the result of many engineer-years.
Anything where torch.compile is on by default and the operation is purely elementwise. The compiler already does the fusion.

You will probably win or tie on:

RMSNorm at typical hidden sizes once fused with the residual add.
FlashAttention forward at seq >= 1024, even on a Turing card.
SwiGLU when fused with its biases, vs PyTorch’s three-kernel default path.



33.4.5 If you complete this
You have earned the title “Triton kernel writer” for transformer/LLM work. Add your numbers to a README, name the GPU, name the version of PyTorch and Triton, and ship it. From here, the only thing left is to pick up Hopper-specific features (TMA, WGMMA, FP8), and that is a different book.
If you cannot complete this yet — that is fine. The 30-day plan above is designed to get you here. Walk back the gap to the chapter you skimmed too fast and read it slower this time.

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text: 34.1 Phase 1: Design

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text:
Write the operation out in plain math. Name every tensor, list every shape, and pin down every dtype.
Write a PyTorch reference implementation first. Make it as obvious and unoptimized as possible. This is your oracle.
Enumerate the input/output shapes and dtypes you intend to support.
Identify which dimensions are reduced, which are mapped over, and which are independent.
Decide what work one program instance is responsible for (one row, one tile, one head, etc.).
Decide the grid shape — usually ceil(N / BLOCK_SIZE) along whichever axes the kernel maps over.
Decide the block size constants. Start with powers of two; you can autotune later.
Decide the accumulator dtype. For matmul and reductions on FP16/BF16 inputs, accumulate in FP32.
Decide what gets loaded into SRAM (tiles) and what stays in registers (small vectors, scalars).
If the kernel does multi-stage software pipelining (matmul-style), plan num_stages up front.
Sketch the numerical hazards: overflow, underflow, catastrophic cancellation, division by tiny numbers. Note the mitigations (e.g., subtract the row max before exp in softmax).

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text:
34.2 Phase 2: Implement

Write the kernel signature: input pointers, output pointer, sizes, strides, BLOCK_SIZE as tl.constexpr.
Compute pid = tl.program_id(axis=...) for each grid axis.
Compute base offsets from pid and strides. Pass strides in as kernel arguments — do not hardcode row_stride = N.
Build per-element offset vectors with tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE).
Build masks for any dimension whose extent is not a multiple of the block size.
Use tl.load(ptr, mask=mask, other=safe_default) — pick other so a masked-off lane cannot poison a reduction (0.0 for sums, -inf for maxes).
Do the actual compute. Keep it readable; cleverness comes after correctness.
tl.store(ptr, value, mask=mask).
Write the Python launcher: allocate output, compute grid, call kernel. Validate input contiguity / dtype where assumed.

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text:
34.3 Phase 3: Test

Write a tiny-shape test (e.g., N=7, M=3) that you can reason about by hand. This catches stride and mask bugs before anything else.
Add a power-of-two shape test that should hit happy paths.
Add a non-power-of-two shape test that forces the mask to be exercised.
Add a boundary test: extent equal to BLOCK_SIZE, extent equal to BLOCK_SIZE + 1, extent equal to BLOCK_SIZE - 1.
Test each dtype variant the kernel claims to support (fp16, bf16, fp32, etc.) with the right tolerance for each.
If you claim to support non-contiguous inputs, test with a transposed or sliced tensor.
Compare against the PyTorch reference with torch.testing.assert_close and dtype-appropriate rtol / atol.
If the op has a backward, test it via torch.autograd.gradcheck (small fp64 inputs) or against the PyTorch backward.
Add a determinism check if relevant: run the kernel twice on the same input and assert bitwise equality.

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text:
34.4 Phase 4: Optimize

Establish a baseline: how long does the unoptimized kernel take, and what fraction of memory bandwidth or peak FLOPs is that?
Define the bound: is the kernel memory-bound, compute-bound, or latency-bound? Roofline-style math beats guessing.
Try larger BLOCK_SIZE values. Bigger tiles reduce overhead but cost registers and shared memory.
Try num_warps variations (1, 2, 4, 8). More warps help latency hiding; fewer help register pressure.
For matmul-style kernels, try num_stages variations (2–5).
Wrap the kernel with triton.autotune over a small set of configs that span the realistic shape space.
Re-measure with triton.testing.do_bench — warmup, sync, percentile reporting.
If memory-bound, look for fusion opportunities (combine with the surrounding op).
If compute-bound, check that you are using tensor cores (matmul) and that the accumulator dtype is right.

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
text:
34.5 Phase 5: Document

Document the kernel’s signature, supported shapes, supported dtypes, and the layout assumptions.
Document the hardware assumptions (e.g., “requires Hopper for FP8”).
Document the numerical contract: tolerance versus the PyTorch reference, and why.
Record the benchmark numbers you actually measured, the GPU you measured on, and the shape you measured at. Do not extrapolate.
Note any known limitations or future work in a # TODO comment so the next reader is not surprised.

title: 34  Triton Kernel Design Checklist
section: 34.6 Common-bug audit (read this before declaring the kernel “done”)
text:
34.6 Common-bug audit (read this before declaring the kernel “done”)

Did you forget a mask on the last partial tile?
Did you load with other=0.0 into a max reduction (should be -inf)?
Did you load with other=-inf into a sum reduction (should be 0.0)?
Did you hardcode a stride that should have come from tensor.stride(...)?
Did you accumulate FP16 inputs in FP16 (should usually be FP32)?
Did you use tl.exp on a value that wasn’t first shifted by the max (overflow risk)?
Did you assume contiguity but the caller passed a transposed tensor?
Did you assume the input is on the GPU but the test runs on CPU?
Did you forget torch.cuda.synchronize() before timing?
Did you forget warmup runs before benchmarking?
Did you treat BLOCK_SIZE as a runtime variable instead of tl.constexpr?
Did you off-by-one the grid dimension ((N + BS - 1) // BS vs N // BS)?
Did you write to the output without a mask, scribbling past the last valid element?
